Iliad Intensive CurriculumIliad

Physics of Deep Learning

These notes are meant to serve as an introduction to physics-inspired analysis and inquiry in deep learning, particularly focusing on techniques from statistical mechanics, statistical field theory, and (a bit of) dynamical systems. A major theme throughout is scale — how neural networks behave as various hyperparameters (e.g. width, depth, total number of weights, dataset size, training algorithm, learning rate, training time, etc.) are taken to extremes. Such extreme 'macroscopic' limits often clarify structural aspects of learning, enabling relatively simple analytic approximations of otherwise complicated 'microscopic' systems. We will review some classic ideas in statistical learning theory, and key early results on large-scale behavior of neural networks, such as the Gaussian-process limit at initialization, and lazy learning/NTK regime during training. We will also survey some more recent successes of physics in deep learning, such as mean-field-theory methods applied to shallow networks, Bayesian learning, and stochastic dynamical systems (DMFT). We will also discuss 'neural scaling laws' for optimal training and various proposed derivations, many of which require only elementary back-of-the-envelope calculations. We don't assume any physics background, though reading some of the suggested reference material may be helpful. We do assume a basic understanding of probability theory, Bayesian inference, and simple neural networks (MLP's), as well as undergraduate-level calculus, linear algebra, and (in a few places) differential geometry. Some of the material here overlaps with the notes on learning dynamics and deep linear networks. The document is currently still evolving, particularly in Sections 5-7. Sections 5 and 7 have been largely generated by Claude Fable, with detailed human prompting and subsequent editing.

By Aleksander Czejdo (Iliad Fellow), Tudor Dimofte (Iliad & Timaeus Fellow; University of Edinburgh), Brianna Grado-White (Iliad Fellow), Charles Renshaw-Whitman (Iliad Fellow)

What you’ll learn

By the end of these notes, you should be able to:

  • Use the statistical-mechanics dictionary for Bayesian learning — energy, entropy, action, free energy, order parameters, quenched averages — and compute the annealed learning curve of the teacher–student perceptron.
  • Explain what a phase transition is, why finite systems show smooth sigmoids and growing susceptibility peaks instead of true kinks, and how the Ising perceptron realizes a first-order transition to perfect generalization, metastable lag included.
  • Derive the Gaussian-process description of a wide network at initialization, and explain the roles of fan-in initialization, the depth-to-width ratio, and the edge of chaos.
  • Derive the NTK, and explain why it freezes at large width — so that training reduces to kernel regression, with no feature learning.
  • Derive, heuristically, the mean-field limit of one-hidden-layer networks — neurons as interacting particles, self-consistency, the McKean–Vlasov equation — and explain how its moving kernel encodes feature learning; place the NTK and mean-field limits on the scaling dial, and connect it to μP and hyperparameter transfer.
  • Compare the two theoretical accounts of grokking — an equilibrium first-order transition vs. delayed lazy-to-rich dynamics — and propose an experiment that would distinguish them.
  • Recognize the MSRJD/DMFT path-integral formulation of training dynamics, the role of correlation and response functions, and double descent as a dynamical phase transition.
  • Derive the three scaling laws of the quantization model, explain "emergence" as the aggregation of staggered cliffs, and survey where scaling exponents come from: skill statistics, data geometry, and kernel spectra.

1. Intro reading: learning mechanics

The review (Simon et al. 2026) argues that a scientific theory of deep learning — a "mechanics of learning" — is already emerging, and it organizes the evidence into five converging strands: analytically solvable settings, insightful limits, simple empirical laws, disentangled hyperparameters, and universal phenomena. The body of the paper develops the first two strands in detail and samples the remaining three. These notes will do much the same, so it is worth keeping the five strands in mind as a map of everything that follows.

The paper's starting observation deserves to be savored, because it sets the tone for the whole subject. A deep learning system is completely specified by four explicit ingredients: an architecture (a composition of simple linear and nonlinear maps), a dataset, an objective, and a learning rule (gradient-based updates from a random initialization). Nothing is hidden: every parameter, every gradient, every intermediate activation can be measured, at every step, to whatever precision we like. In the language of the reading, deep learning directly exposes its own equations of motion — the central challenge is not opacity but complexity. This places the field in very different territory from the genuinely opaque sciences: in neuroscience or cell biology the microscopic equations of motion are unknown and the state is largely unmeasurable, while in high-energy physics we must infer the microscopic laws indirectly, from scattering amplitudes. The better analogy is fluid dynamics: there, too, we possess the microscopic law — for deep learning, the update equation is five lines of code — and what is missing is the effective description, the analogue of Navier–Stokes.

Read Section 2 (only) of (Simon et al. 2026), and think about the following:

  1. Rank the physics analogies in Table 1 of the reading (solvable models ↔ hydrogen atom; limits ↔ thermodynamic limit; empirical laws ↔ Kepler and Planck; hyperparameters ↔ Reynolds number; universality ↔ critical phenomena). Which are the most compelling? Which do you think are most useful in understanding deep learning?
  2. Discretization and other approximations. The reading's Discretization Hypothesis proposes that practical networks are best understood as noisy, finite approximations to models of infinite size — like a finite-difference discretization of a PDE — so that finite-size effects typically cost performance rather than enable it. Given what you've seen so far, does this seem accurate? The hypothesis is falsifiable: it would be refuted by a finite-size effect that delivers a general benefit unachievable in any limit. What are some possible experiments/setups that could falsify it?
  3. What actually matters for alignment? The reading wants falsifiable, quantitative, average-case predictions rather than worst-case bounds — physics rather than classical learning theory. What is lost? E.g. for alignment, does one want worst-case guarantees or forecasting of typical capabilities? Which of the five lines of evidence is most relevant for alignment?

You may want to revisit these questions at later stages as you go through these notes, and learn more about physics-inspired approaches in deep learning.

2. Statistical mechanics of learning

There is a large and well-developed body of work applying physics techniques to learning theory. Much of it consists of statistical mechanics applied to Bayesian learning; the classic textbook treatment is Engel and Van den Broeck (Engel & Van den Broeck 2001), and modern reviews include (Zdeborov'a & Krzakala 2016; Bahri et al. 2020). An excellent reference for the physics behind this material is David Tong's Part III lecture course (Tong 2012). In this section we review a few of the key ideas from this tradition — order parameters, free energies, quenched averages, phase transitions — and we will keep returning to them throughout the notes.

We introduce the terminology through a single running example, simple enough that every step can be done explicitly.

2.1 Example: the teacher-student perceptron

We consider a simple setup whose inputs are d-dimensional vectors x∈Rd sampled from a normal distribution N(0,Id​), and whose outputs are {±1}, with truth given by

y=sign(w∗⋅x)(for some fixed w∗∈Rd)

The goal is to learn the weights w∗. We'll do this by fitting training data (xμ,yμ)μ=1n​ with a model

fw​(x)=sign(w⋅x)(w to be learned).

In classical learning theory, w∗ is called the "teacher," and w is called the "student." The number of parameters of the student model is N=d. We can reduce the parameter count by 1 by noticing that there is a symmetry w→λw (λ>0) under which fw​(x) remains invariant. To eliminate the symmetry, we'll require the parameters to live on a sphere, ∣w∗∣2=∣w∣2=N. This is sometimes called the spherical perceptron. The normalization by N is so that each individual wi​ remains of order one.

The thermodynamic limit. In physics, there is a notion of degrees of freedom of a statistical system, which matches the parameters (N−1 independent weights here) in a learning setup. One considers behavior of a system as the degrees of freedom become large, N→∞, which is called the thermodynamic limit.

  • Extensive quantities are ones that grow proportional to N, e.g. inner products such as w⋅w∗ in our example.
  • Intensive quantities are ones that remain finite as N→∞. These are typically densities, measured per degree of freedom; for example, individual weights wi​, or ratios (w⋅w∗)/N.

In our example we will also send the number of training examples n→∞. We'll see that the way the model learns depends on the ratio of examples per parameter, known as the load

α=n/N.

The order parameter. An order parameter is a macroscopic quantity that summarizes the microscopic state for the purposes of the questions asked (typically at large N). An important order parameter here is the overlap

R=cosϑ:=Nw⋅w∗​∈[−1,1],

the cosine of the angle between student and teacher. R fully characterizes the success of the model, in a precise sense, due to the following symmetry argument. The input distribution N(0,IN​) and the uniform measure on the sphere are invariant under the orthogonal group O(N), so any quantity defined by averaging over inputs — the generalization error below, the volume computations to come — is invariant under simultaneous rotation of (w,w∗). The complete list of rotation invariants of the pair is ∣w∣2, ∣w∗∣2, and w⋅w∗; and the first two are fixed by the spherical constraint, leaving R. Any rotation-invariant function of (w,w∗) is a function of R alone.

Generalization error. The generalization error of a student is the probability of disagreeing with the teacher on a fresh input. It's an expectation over the full data distribution:

ε(w)=Px∼N(0,IN​)​[sign(w⋅x)=sign(w∗⋅x)].

By the symmetry argument this is a function of R alone, and it has a clean geometric form. Decomposing the input x into components parallel to and orthogonal to the 2d plane spanned by w and w∗,

x=x∥​+x⊥​

we observe that x⊥​ doesn't affect either sign sign(w⋅x) or sign(w∗⋅x). Since x has an isotropic Gaussian

1

distribution, the projection x∥​ is an isotropic (2d) Gaussian as well. The region in the plane where sign(w⋅x)=sign(w∗⋅x) is a double wedge, sitting between two lines in the plane that meet at an angle ϑ=arccosR. The probability that sign(w⋅x)=sign(w∗⋅x) is therefore

ε(R)=πϑ​=π1​arccos(R).

The answer is independent of N because only the two-dimensional projection ever entered. At large N,n, the learning problem reduces to how ε (or the typical overlap R) varies with the load α.

2.2 Bayesian learning and a physics dictionary

We'll "train" our model using Bayesian inference. We assume a prior distribution on weights w that's uniform on the sphere, with measure denoted π(w)dw. Given a single data sample (xμ,yμ), the probability that fw​(xμ)=yμ, conditioned on the weights w, is (trivially)

P(fw​(xμ)=yμ​w)=Θ(yμ(w⋅xμ)),Θ(u):={10​ifu≥0u<0​,

where Θ is the step function. Therefore, after seeing n samples, the Bayesian posterior on weights is

P(w)=Z1​μ=1∏n​Θ(yμ(w⋅xμ))π(w),Z=∫dwP(w),

with a normalization constant Z (the Bayesian marginal likelihood of the data).

In a statistical mechanics context:

  • Energy is minus the log-likelihood of a hypothesis (a weight w). Here the likelihood is either 0 or 1, and energy E=−log∏μ=1n​Θ(yμ(w⋅xμ)) just tracks whether a hypothesis is ever violated by the data. (Note: we are at zero temperature, meaning constraints are hard. At positive temperature one would tolerate violations at a price, e.g. encoded in a smooth loss function. See Sec. 2.5 for more.)
  • Gibbs measure/posterior ∝e−energy is the probability measure inferred in hypotheses.
  • Partition function Z is the normalizing constant of the Gibbs measure.
  • Entropy is the log-volume of hypotheses with a given property, e.g. the weights w with a given R. Large entropy = many hypotheses.
  • Free energy and free energy density (or average free energy per degree of freedom)
F=−logZ,φ=NF​=−N1​logZ.

In physics, F gets minimized as a system equilibrates. Note that F is extensive (it scales with N), whereas φ is intensive, and has a limit as N→∞.

  • Quenched free energy (density)
Φ=Edata​(φ)

is averaged over training draws from the entire dataset. The name comes from the physics term for fixing/averaging the randomness of a system before letting its dynamics run, much as impurities are frozen into an alloy when it is quenched in water.

There are a few reasons to care about the free energy. See Tong's notes (Tong 2012; Tong 2012) for a full discussion; here we mention three important properties. First, F is naturally an extensive quantity, whereas Z is neither extensive nor intensive. Second, at large N, we expect behavior of our learning model to depend only on a small number of order parameters (here, the overlap R). The Gibbs posterior P(w) induces (or "pushes forward" to) an effective probability distribution on the order parameters, P(R), with Z=∫dRP(R). In a typical situation, the probability P(R) will be concentrated in a few different regions Ui​ in the space of order parameters, so that

Z≈i∑​e−Fi​,Fi​:=−log[∫Ui​​dRP(R)]

The region with the lowest local free energy dominates the entire partition function — that's the sense in which one should minimize F.

Third, the derivatives of the free energy control expectation values of order parameters and other observables. One may ask: derivatives with respect to what? At first glance, Z and F are just numbers. However, they depend on hyperparameters of the model (such as N,n in our example), and this dependence forms the basis for the study of phase transitions (see Section 2.4). Moreover, it is common to extend Z,F to generating functions of desired observables by adding so-called source terms.

To illustrate source terms in our example, suppose we were interested in the expectation values of various powers of the overlap R,R2,R3... under the Gibbs posterior P(w). Consider a modified partition function

Z(J)=∫dwP(w)eJR(w),F(J)=−logZ(J),

now depending on an extra variable J. Then

Ew∼P(w)​(R(w))=−∂J∂​F(J)​J=0​,Varw∼P(w)​(R(w))=−∂J2∂2​F(J)​J=0​,

and higher derivatives yield higher so-called cumulants. (See also Section 3.3.)

Exercise 2.1 (Sources and cumulants). Verify the formulas (2.14) by direct differentiation. Then show that, in general, the p-th derivative of −F(J)=logZ(J) at J=0 computes the p-th cumulant of R: the mean, the variance, the third central moment, and — starting at p=4 — combinations of moments (such as E[(R−ER)4]−3Var(R)2) that vanish whenever R is Gaussian. Cumulants will return, wearing field-theory clothing, in Section 3.3.

Solution

Differentiating under the integral, ∂J​logZ(J)=Z(J)1​∫dwP(w)R(w)eJR(w)=EJ​[R], which at J=0 is the posterior mean; this is the first formula of (2.14) since F=−logZ. Differentiating once more, ∂J2​logZ=EJ​[R2]−EJ​[R]2=VarJ​(R), giving the second. In general logZ(J) is the cumulant generating function of R: its Taylor coefficients are κ1​=E[R], κ2​=Var(R), κ3​=E[(R−ER)3], and κ4​=E[(R−ER)4]−3Var(R)2, which one checks by expanding logE[eJR] in powers of J and matching moments. For Gaussian R, logZ(J) is exactly quadratic in J, so all κp​ with p>2 vanish — which is why higher cumulants measure non-Gaussianity, the theme of Section 3.3.

Finally, we note that quenching — taking an expectation value over all draws of the training data — is a natural approximation at large dataset size n. Quenching should be done on the free energy, not the partition function, since it's the former that's an extensive quantity, and it's the former that controls expectation values. For example, averaging EP​(R) from (2.14) over dataset draws, we get

Edata​EP​(R)=−∂J∂​[Edata​F(J)]​J=0​=−N∂J∂​Φ(J)​J=0.​

2.3 The annealed approximation

We'll now illustrate the idea of "minimizing F at large N and n" in the case of our simple example, the spherical perceptron. Since we're at large n, we use the quenched free energy: we want to analyze Ex∼q​logZ, where q=N(0,IN​) is the data distribution.

Unfortunately, averaging logZ is still hard. Averaging Z turns out to be much easier, and The so-called annealed approximation swaps them:

Ex∼q​logZ⟶≈​logEx∼q​Z.

Let's use the latter.

Since the data samples are i.i.d., the average of (2.9) over the data factorizes across examples; and each example is satisfied by a student at overlap R with probability 1−ε(R) (the probability that teacher and student agree on a random input — the complement of Equation 2.7). Therefore,

Ex∼q​Z=∫dwπ(w)(1−ε(R(w)))n.

Next, we'd like to "push forward" the distribution π(w)dw (the uniform measure on a sphere SN−1 of radius N​) to a distribution over overlaps R. For any function g(R(w)) depending on w only through R, we can factor the integral over w as

∫w∈SN−1​dwπ(w)g(R(w))=∫R∈[−1,1]​dRg(R)=:exp(Nh(R))∫ws.t.R(w)=R​dwπ(w)​​.

As indicated, we define h(R) to be 1/N times the log-volume of the slice of the sphere SN−1 where R(w)=R. Physically, this is an entropy. To compute it, decompose w=Rw∗+w⊥​ with w⊥​⊥w∗; the spherical constraint gives ∣w⊥​∣2=N(1−R2), so the slice at fixed R is a sphere of radius N(1−R2)​ in the (N−1)-dimensional orthogonal complement, with volume ∝(N(1−R2))(N−2)/2. Therefore,

h(R)=21​log(1−R2)+const+O(N1​logN).

Now consider N very large. To exponential accuracy in 1/N, we keep the term of order N in the exponent and drop terms of order logN and below (Jacobians, prefactors, the surface-area constant). Then

EZ≈∫−11​dRe−NSann​(R),Sann​(R):=−entropy21​log(1−R2)​​energy−αlog(1−ε(R))​​,

where α=n/N is the load parameter introduced earlier. Borrowing another term from physics, we will call Sann​ the (annealed) action. The name comes from the field-theory formalism described later in Section 2.6 and Section 3.3; one can also think of the action as a local free energy density S(ann)​=φ(R), depending on R as well as the other hyperparameters of the problem.

As N→∞, we evaluate the annealed partition function with a saddle point approximation (a.k.a. stationary phase, a.k.a. Laplace's method). For an integral ∫e−NS(R)dR with N→∞, the integrand is exponentially peaked at the minimizer R∗​ of S; the region within ∼1/N​ of R∗​ contributes everything, and

N1​log∫e−NS(R)dRN→∞​−Rmin​S(R).

Thus,

Φ(α)=Rmin​Sann​(R)+o(1).

The two terms of Sann​ stage an entropy–energy competition, a central theme of statistical mechanics. Intuitively: the first term counts how many students sit at overlap R — it is lowest at R=0, because in high dimension almost all of the sphere is nearly orthogonal to any fixed direction (concentration of measure), and it pulls the minimum toward the typical, the numerous, the disordered. The second term measures how well such students fit the data — it is lowest at R=1 and pulls toward the special, the accurate, the ordered. Neither wins outright; the compromise moves with α, which weights the data term. In physics the same structure appears with energy in place of data-fit and temperature in place of 1/α; ordered phases (magnets, crystals) form when the energy term wins. Here: for small α the minimum sits near R=0; as α grows it moves smoothly toward 1. Figure 1 shows the action Sann​(R) for a series of loads α∈[0,1]: a single minimum, drifting continuously.

The large-α asymptotics can be read off by expanding near R=1. Writing R=cos(πε) so that ε is the generalization error itself, 1−R2≈(πε)2, and

Sann​≈−log(πε)+αε+const,

whose minimum is at

εann​(α)≃α1​.

Learning curves decay as a power law in the amount of data, with exponent 1 (meaning ε≃1/αc with c=1). We have found our first scaling law!

Exercise 2.2 (Annealed learning curve). Fill in the steps of the annealed calculation: derive Equation 2.7, the sphere-slice entropy h(R), and the saddle-point condition of Equation 2.22; verify Equation 2.24. Then show that at small α the annealed theory predicts R∝α, and sketch the full annealed learning curve.

Solution

The wedge formula. Project x onto the plane spanned by w and w∗; the projection is an isotropic two-dimensional Gaussian, and the orthogonal components affect neither sign. The two decision boundaries are diameters of this plane meeting at angle ϑ=arccosR, and the signs disagree exactly when the projected point lands in the double wedge between them, of total angular measure 2ϑ out of 2π: ε=ϑ/π.

The slice entropy. Decompose w=Rw∗+w⊥​. The spherical constraint ∣w∣2=N forces ∣w⊥​∣2=N(1−R2), so the slice at fixed R is a sphere of radius N(1−R2)​ in the (N−1)-dimensional orthogonal complement, of volume ∝(N(1−R2))(N−2)/2=e2N​log(1−R2)+O(logN), giving h(R)=21​log(1−R2) up to constants.

The saddle-point condition. Setting Sann′​(R)=0 with ε(R)=arccos(R)/π gives

1−R2R​=π1−R2​(1−ε(R))α​⟺1−R2​R​=π(1−ε(R))α​.

Large α. With R=cos(πε) and ε→0: 1−R2=sin2(πε)≈(πε)2, so Sann​≈−log(πε)+αε+const, minimized at ε=1/α.

Small α. For small R: the entropic part of the action is ≈R2/2 and ε(R)≈21​−R/π, so −αlog(1−ε)≈−αlog21​−π2α​R, and minimizing R2/2−π2α​R gives R∗=2α/π∝α. The full learning curve therefore rises linearly from R=0, bends over, and approaches R=1 with the power-law tail ε≃1/α.

2.3.1 Optional: what the annealed approximation gets wrong

The exact treatment of the spherical perceptron (Seung et al. 1992; Engel & Van den Broeck 2001) yields

εGibbs​(α)≃α0.625​,

same exponent as Equation 2.24, different constant. Why does annealing err, and in which direction? Jensen's inequality always guarantees that logEZ≥ElogZ, so annealed free energy is an overestimate. To see what drives the gap, note that Z is a random variable (it depends on the dataset) of the form Z=e−Nφ where φ fluctuates from dataset to dataset. Exponentiating turns modest fluctuations of φ into enormous fluctuations of Z: a dataset whose φ exceeds the typical value by a constant is exponentially rare, but contributes an exponentially large Z, and the two exponentials compete at the same order. The average EZ can therefore be dominated by vanishingly rare datasets — in our problem, weakly informative datasets that happen to leave an unusually large contribution to the Z integral — while the typical dataset behaves quite differently. (This is the same phenomenon as for lognormal random variables, where the mean can sit far in the upper tail of the distribution; the mean is a bad summary of a heavy-tailed quantity.)

This also predicts the direction of the error, qualitatively. The rare datasets that dominate EZ are those that constrain the student unusually weakly; weakly constrained students sit at lower overlap. The annealed average thus overweights poorly aligned students and overestimates the generalization error, 1/α>0.625/α.

Remark: Scaling exponents will not always survive annealing, as they did here. Here the model is realizable (a teacher exists), fluctuations of φ are tame, and annealing errs only in the constant. In general the annealed computation can fail qualitatively — most famously for models with discrete weights at large load, where it can predict negative entropies (fewer than one consistent student, nonsense for a count) and spurious transition points.

2.3.2 Optional: the replica method

The full, non-annealed calculation computes Edata​logZ directly, via the identity

ElogZ=Q→0lim​QEZQ−1​(from ZQ=enlogZ=1+QlogZ+O(Q2)).

The strategy is to compute EZQ for integer Q, where it has a transparent meaning, obtain a formula analytic in Q, and continue it to Q→0. For integer Q, there are Q independent copies (replicas) of the student, all judged against the same dataset:

EZQ=E∫a=1∏Q​dwaπ(wa)μ=1∏n​a=1∏Q​Θ(yμ(wa⋅xμ)):

Averaging over the shared data is what couples the replicas. Each example μ couples to the replicas only through the Q+1 scalars ua=wa⋅xμ/N​ and v=w∗⋅xμ/N​, which are jointly Gaussian with covariance determined entirely by the overlap matrix

qab=Nwa⋅wb​,Ra=Nwa⋅w∗​

The data average factorizes across the n examples, each contributing an identical factor, which assembles to e−ne(q,R)=e−αNe(q,R); the w-integrals at fixed overlaps contribute an entropic factor eNh(q,R) by the same slice-counting as Equation 2.19. Saddle-point approximation then leads to

−N1​logEZQ=q,Rmin​[−h(q,R)+αe(q,R)]+o(1).

One retains an interaction among replicas, encoded in the matrix qab.

Replica symmetry. A common and useful ansatz in solving these equations, called replica symmetry, is to take qab=q (all a=b), Ra=R. This is a natural choice, because the saddle-point equations themselves are symmetric under permuting replicas. As a caution, however, symmetric equations can admit asymmetric solutions. This happens in physical systems, famously in the analysis of spin glasses. For our simple example, replica symmetry can be carefully justified using convexity of the regions where the energy landscape ∏μ​Θ(yμ(w⋅xμ)) is nonzero.

The following optional exercise completes the remainder of the quenched calculation leading to Equation 2.25, at the level of structure rather than of every Gaussian integral. The full details may be found in (Engel & Van den Broeck 2001, chs. 2–3).

Exercise 2.3 (The quenched calculation, via replicas (optional)). Work through the following program, in as much detail as your appetite allows.

(a) Replicate. For integer Q, write EZQ=E∫∏a=1Q​dwaπ(wa)∏μ,a​Θ(yμwa⋅xμ): an n-fold copy of the system coupled only through the shared data.

(b) Average over data. Each example couples to the replicas only through the Q+1 jointly Gaussian fields ua=wa⋅x/N​ and v=w∗⋅x/N​, whose covariance is fixed by the overlap matrix

qab=Nwa⋅wb​,Ra=Nwa⋅w∗​.

The data average factorizes across the n examples, each contributing the same function of (qab,Ra): the disorder is gone, at the price of coupling the replicas.

(c) Push forward to the order parameters. Insert delta functions fixing qab and Ra; the w-integrals become an entropic factor eNh(q,R), and Equation 2.22 is generalized to a saddle-point problem over matrices, EZQ≈∫dqdRe−N[−h(q,R)+αe(q,R)].

(d) Replica symmetry. Take the ansatz qab=q for all a=b, Ra=R. The free energy becomes an explicit function of two scalars (involving the Gaussian tail function H(x)=∫x∞​2π​dz​e−z2/2), analytically continued in Q, and differentiated at Q=0.

(e) Use the symmetry of Gibbs learning. A student drawn uniformly from the version space is statistically indistinguishable from the teacher (both are "typical" consistent vectors), which forces q=R at the saddle: the overlap between two Gibbs students equals their overlap with the teacher. One scalar remains.

(f) Solve and expand. The saddle-point equation for R(α) is transcendental; solve numerically for the full learning curve, and expand at large α to extract ε≃0.625/α.

Solution

The six steps are their own outline; we record only the checkpoints. (Step 2) The covariance of (u1,...,uQ,v) is E[uaub]=qab, E[uav]=Ra, E[v2]=1, so the per-example factor is e−e(q,R), with energy density e(q,R)=−logP[all Q replicas agree with the teacher], minus the log of a (Q+1)-dimensional Gaussian orthant probability. (Step 4) Under the replica-symmetric ansatz this orthant probability reduces to a one-dimensional integral over the shared Gaussian "field," producing the tail function H; the free energy per replica then has a finite Q→0 limit by design. (Step 5) The symmetry argument — a uniformly drawn consistent student is statistically equivalent to the teacher — forces q=R, collapsing the saddle to one equation. (Step 6) Numerically solving it and expanding at large α gives ε≃0.625/α, the quoted 38% improvement in the constant over the annealed bound. Full details: (Engel & Van den Broeck 2001, chs. 2–3).

2.4 Phase transitions

A phase transition is a value of a control parameter (in our example, the load α; in physics, temperature or pressure) at which the limiting free energy per degree of freedom, φ(α)=F(α)/N, fails to be analytic, so that some macroscopic observable changes abruptly. Genuine non-analyticity can only occur in the thermodynamic limit: at any finite N, the partition function is a finite integral of analytic functions of α, so F is analytic too. What a finite system exhibits instead is a rapid but smooth crossover that sharpens as N grows.

We'll take a moment to walk through the basic structure of a so-called first-order phase transition. This is the most common example, and one can find its fingerprint all over statistical physics and statistical learning. A first-order transition is characterized by two distinct phases exchanging dominance. At infinite N, it shows up as a discontinuity in the first derivative of the free energy, as a control parameter crosses its critical value.

Let's work with a general, abstract model, in which the partition function takes the form

Z=∫dRe−NS(R;α),

in terms of a control parameter α (think: some combination of hyperparameters of a model, which can be tuned) and some order parameter(s) R that capture macroscopic information about the model's weights. What will actually be relevant is a different order parameter, given by the first derivative of the action

O(R;α):=∂α∂​S(R;α).

For example, in (2.20), we'd have O=−log(1−ε(R)) (a simple function or R itself).

To get a classic first-order transition, we also need to assume that S(R;α) has developed two separated (regular) local minima, at R1​(α) and R2​(α). These correspond to the two competing phases. Let Si​(α):=S(Ri​(α);α) be the values of the action in these phases. At large N, the partition function is dominated by the minima,

Z≈e−NS1​(α)+e−NS2​(α),

and the relative probabilities of finding the system in each phase are

pi​(α)=e−NS1​(α)+e−NS2​(α)e−NSi​(α)​.

Now suppose that the two local minima cross at some αc​, that is,

⎩⎨⎧​S1​(α)=S2​(α)S1​(α)<S2​(α)S1​(α)>S2​(α)​α=αc​α<αc​α>αc​​,

where ∂α​S1​>∂α​S2​ at αc​. Expanding to first order in Δα:=α−αc​:

S1​−S2​≈ΔS′⋅Δα,ΔS′:=∂α​S1​−∂α​S2​,
⟹p1​(α)≈1+eNΔS′Δα1​,p2​(α)≈1+e−NΔS′Δα1​.

Thus close to αc​, the occupation of the phases is a logistic, or sigmoid function of NΔS′Δα. Note that at finite N the system swaps from concentrating its probability in one basin to the other smoothly, but over a window of width δα∼1/(NΔS′) that shrinks as N grows.

It's useful to characterize the change in phase in terms of the expectation value of the new order parameter O=∂α​S. A short computation from (2.33) gives

E(O)=∂α∂φ​≈p1​∂α​S1​+p2​∂α​S2​≈{∂α​S1​∂α​S2​​α≪αc​α≫αc​​.

Thus, as α crosses αc​, E(O) interpolates from ∂α​S1​ to ∂α​S2​ across the same logistic curve we saw in p1​,p2​ — a sigmoid of height ΔS′ and width ∼1/(NΔS′). As N→∞, φ(α) remains continuous, but has a kink at αc​, leading to a jump in the order parameter O.

It's also interesting to differentiate (2.38) once more, using ∂α​p1​=−∂α​p2​≈−Np1​p2​ΔS′, to find

χ:=−∂α∂​E(O)=−∂α2∂2φ​=Np1​p2​(ΔS′)2−p1​∂α2​S1​−p2​∂α2​S2​.

The quantity χ is the analogue of a heat capacity or susceptibility (in thermodynamics the heat capacity is −T∂2F/∂T2). The first term on the RHS of (2.39) is the interesting one. Near αc​, where p1​p2​≈41​, the first term has a peak of height N(ΔS′)2/4, concentrated in a window of width 1/N; it diverges and approximates a delta-function as N→∞.

Figure Figure 2 shows the behavior of all three quantities φ=F/N, ∂α​φ, and −∂α2​φ at once. Watching the peak in −∂α2​φ grow with N, rather than saturate, is the standard numerical diagnostic that separates a genuine first-order transition from a mere crossover. The smoothed-sigmoid plot of ∂α​φ is worth remembering whenever "emergent capabilities" in models of growing size is under discussion (such as in Section 7.3).

We have focused on a simple first-order transition, because it's the most prominent kind, and recurs several times in these notes. In general, an n-th order transition is characterized by a discontinuity in some n-th derivative of the free energy with respect to control parameters. A classic example of a second-order transition occurs in the Curie–Weiss magnet of Exercise 5.1 at specially tuned values of the temperature and magnetic field; see also (Tong 2012) for further intuition.

Remarks: The derivation above used nothing but the existence of two competing minima whose local actions cross: the microscopics of the model enter only through the two functions Si​(α). This is why first-order phenomenology is so universal. Second, the equilibrium analysis with weights (2.34) say nothing about evolution in time. Dynamics that carry the system from one basin to the other can take exponentially long to do it, leaving the system stuck in the thermodynamically subdominant phase. This phenomenon is known as metastability, or hysteresis, and we will meet it again in Section 5.7, in the context of grokking.

Is there a phase transition in our spherical-perceptron example? No. The action Sann​(R) (and its quenched counterpart) has a unique minimum for every α, moving smoothly (Figure 1); φ(α) is analytic, the learning curve ε(α) is smooth, and learning is gradual. The reason is visible in Equation 2.20: the entropic part −21​log(1−R2) of the action diverges to +∞ as R→1, so the perfectly aligned state is infinitely penalized and the minimum always sits in the interior, sliding continuously. We can produce a transition by using a model in which the perfectly aligned state carries finite entropy. We give an example of this next, by discretizing the spherical perceptron.

2.4.1 Example: the Ising perceptron

Consider the spherical perceptron of Section 2.1, but change one ingredient: let both teacher and student have binary weights,

w,w∗∈{±1}N,

with (obviously) ∣w∣2=∣w∗∣2=N as before. This is sometimes called the Ising perceptron, by analogy with Ising magnetic spins, which take values ±1; however, no other physics of the Ising model will show up here. The data are still generated by Equation 2.1, and the generalization error is unchanged. (That's because for any fixed w with ∣w∣2=N, binary or not, the pair (w⋅x,w∗⋅x)/N​ is jointly Gaussian with correlation R, so the wedge formula Equation 2.7 still gives ε(R)=arccos(R)/π.) Only one thing changes: the entropy of the slice at overlap R becomes a counting problem rather than a continuous volume computation. A student agrees with the teacher on a fraction p=(1+R)/2 of its N coordinates, so the number of students at overlap R is (pNN​), and Stirling's formula gives an entropy density

hI​(R)=N1​log(2(1+R)​NN​)⟶N→∞​H(21+R​),

where H(p)=−plogp−(1−p)log(1−p) the binary entropy function. (We use a subscript $I$' for Ising.') Importantly, at zero overlap hI​(0)=log2, while now at perfect overlap hI​(1)=0 is finite. Intuitively, this is because the perfectly aligned state (student = teacher itself) is actually realized by a discrete configuration, as opposed to being a point on a continuous sphere, which has vanishingly small volume.

The annealed action is assembled exactly as in Equation 2.20:

SI​(R)=−hI​(R)−αlog(1−ε(R)),Φ(α)=R∈[−1,1]min​SI​(R).

We plot SI​(R) in Figure 3, and find the following structure:

  • Perfect alignment. At R=1: the entropy is 0, and ε(1)=0 so the data term (the energy) is also 0. Hence SI​(1)=0 for every α: the perfect state is always available, at exactly zero free energy.
  • Near R=1, with δ=1−R: deviating from the teacher buys entropy, lowering the action by ∼2δ​log(1/δ), but costs data-fit, raising it by αε∼α2δ​/π (expand arccos). Since δ​≫δlog(1/δ), the cost always wins. So R=1 is a local minimum of SI​ at every load.
  • The interior phase. At small α the entropy dominates and SI​ has its global minimum at an interior point R∗(α), with SI​(R∗)<0. (E.g. at α=0 it is at R∗=0, with SI​(R∗)=−log2.) As α grows, this minimum drifts up in R and its value rises toward zero.
  • The crossing. A transition occurs when the two basins exchange dominance: SI​(R∗(αc​))=0=SI​(1). Solving numerically (see Exercise 2.4): αcann​≈1.45, with the interior minimum still sitting at R∗≈0.70, i.e. generalization error ε∗≈0.25. At that load the typical student jumps from 25% error to zero error discontinuously: a first-order transition to perfect generalization.
  • The thermodynamic signature. This is the two-phase mechanism of Section 2.4, verbatim: the interior phase has S1​(α)=SI​(R∗(α)) with slope ∂α​S1​=−log(1−ε(R∗))≈0.29, and the perfectly aligned phase has S2​≡0. So Φ(α)=min(S1​,0) has a kink at αc​, where dΦ/dα drops from ≈0.29 to 0; at finite N the drop is the sigmoid (2.38), of width ∼1/N, and the susceptibility (2.39) shows the growing peak of Figure 2.
  • Hysteresis. Past αc​ the interior minimum survives as a local minimum, out to a about α≈1.73, where it disappears entirely. In the metastable window, learning dynamics that improve teacher-student alignment locally (for just a few wi​) can remain stuck at ε≈0.25, even though the perfect state is thermodynamically dominant: the information to identify the teacher is present in the data before the system can find it. More data eventually helps, abruptly and later than expected.

Exercise 2.4 (★) (The Ising perceptron transition). (a) Derive Equation 2.41 from Stirling's formula. (b) Show that R=1 is a local minimum of SI​ for every α, by the δ​ vs. δlog(1/δ) comparison. (c) Numerically compute Φ(α)=Fann​(α)/N=minR​SI​(R): reproduce Figure 3, locate αcann​, plot the order parameter R∗(α) (with its jump), dΦ/dα (with its kink), and the susceptibility (2.39) (with its peak); and find the point where the interior minimum disappears.

Solution

(a) A student at overlap R agrees with the teacher on pN coordinates with p=(1+R)/2; there are (pNN​) such students, and Stirling gives N1​log(pNN​)→H(p).

(b) With δ=1−R: deviating from the teacher lowers the action by the entropy H(1−2δ​)=2δ​logδ2​+O(δ), which vanishes like δlog(1/δ); but the data term raises it by αε(R)≈α2δ​/π (from arccos(1−δ)≈2δ​), which vanishes only like δ​. Since δ​≫δlog(1/δ) as δ→0, SI​(1−δ)>SI​(1)=0 for small δ at every α>0: the teacher state is always a local minimum.

(c) Minimizing SI​ numerically over the interior and comparing with SI​(1)=0: the interior branch value crosses zero at αcann​≈1.45, where the interior minimizer sits at R∗≈0.70 (ε∗≈0.25); the interior minimum survives as a local (metastable) minimum until the spinodal α≈1.73, exactly as in Figure 3. Plots show R∗(α) jumping from ≈0.70 to 1 at αc​, a drop of dΦ/dα by ≈0.29 — the sigmoid (2.38) at finite N — and the growing susceptibility peak (2.39).

2.5 Bayesian learning vs. SGD for neural networks

In preparation for studying neural networks in the following sections, we'd like to briefly explain

  1. how Bayesian learning, which we've studied so far, generalizes to neural networks;
  2. how Bayesian learning relates, at least heuristically, to SGD (answer: inverse-temperature roughly corresponds to training time);
  3. how practical tests of theory derived from Bayesian learning are performed (namely, by training networks using some version of Langevin dynamics).

Consider a neural network, with parameters θ, that is trained to minimize a loss function

L(θ)=μ=1∑n​ℓθ​(xμ,yμ),

which is a sum of losses for data samples. It's convenient to rewrite this as

L(θ)=nLn​(θ),Ln​(θ)=n1​μ=1∑n​ℓθ​(xμ,yμ),

where Ln​(θ), the "empirical loss," is an average over samples. In statistical physics terms, Ln​ is intensive, remaining order one at large n.

Suppose we are in a situation where at each training step, samples are drawn i.i.d. from the true data distribution. Then we can think of n as a rough measure of training time. As n→∞, we expect the empirical loss to converge to the population loss

n→∞lim​Ln​(θ)=L(θ):=Edata​[ℓθ​(x,y(x))].

For Bayesian inference with a neural network, the likelihood of data {xμ,yμ}μ=1n​ conditioned on weights is not a simple 0 or 1 as in the toy model above. Rather, it's given by

e−βL(θ)=e−nβLn​(θ),

where β is a tunable parameter called the inverse-temperature, which controls the overall "strength" of the loss. Thus, if we start with an initial parameter distribution π(θ) (coming from the choice of random initialization in a neural network) and see n training samples, Bayesian inference says that we should expect a posterior distribution of weights

Pn,β​(θ)=Z1​e−βL(θ)π(θ)=Z1​e−nβLn​(θ)π(θ)

This is a simple generalization of (2.9). It is in fact much closer to the setup one finds in most statistical physics systems, which have states labeled by parameters θ, each at energy E(θ), and a thermal partition function given by the Boltzmann distribution Z=∫dθe−βE(θ), with β=1/T literally the inverse temperature. Equation (2.9) was a degenerate case of this setup at T→0.

Note that in the learning setup (2.47) the sample size n always accompanies the inverse temperature, in the combination nβ. Increasing the number of samples n that have been seen is the same as increasing β (lowering the temperature). Thus, inverse-temperature can be regarded as a rough measure of training time.

In practice, one uses the formula (2.47) (together with a host of classic physics tricks) to derive theoretical properties of the trained system, in various approximations. One does not use the formula directly to actually compute anything, because the loss function is an incredibly complicated function of parameters (as we already know).

Instead, in order to do actual empirical computations that match Bayesian learning, one can train a network via Langevin dynamics. Langevin dynamics is a modified version of stochastic gradient descent, where batch noise is replaced by constant, isotropic Gaussian noise:

discrete optimizerSGD:Δθ=−η(∇θ​L+batch noise)GD:Δθ=−η∇θ​LLD:Δθ=−η∇θ​L+2ηT​ξ​continuous (S)DEθ˙=−η∇θ​L+B​η​Σ(θ)21​dξθ˙=−η∇θ​Lθ˙=−η∇θ​L+2ηT​dξ​​

Here ξ is Gaussian noise with mean 0 and variance I. In Langevin dynamics, with learning rate η, the variance of the noise is normalized by an additional parameter T: the temperature or diffusion constant.

Each of the discrete training algorithms on the left has a continuous-time version on the right. For example, as the length of time steps is scaled down (and the learning rate is scaled up), gradient descent converges to gradient flow, θ˙=−η∇θ​L. Similarly, Langevin dynamics converges to a stochastic differential equation, called the Langevin equation, shown on the bottom-right of (2.48). This is gradient flow together with constant Gaussian noise of relative variance T.

A key feature is that if one starts with an arbitrary distribution of parameters θ and evolves in time with the Langevin equation (and L is a sufficiently nice function), one eventually converges to the Gibbs distribution

Z1​e−βL(θ),

at inverse temperature β=1/T. (See (Tong 2012, Chapter 3) for a physics-focused discussion of this convergence.) Equation (2.49) doesn't automatically include a prior π(θ); but a desired prior can be factored in by adjusting the loss function used in the Langevin equation, L(θ)↦L(θ)−β−1logπ(θ). Thus, one can engineer the parameter distribution (2.47) for Bayesian inference by Langevin training. In practice, the training is done using Langevin dynamics with finite steps, as an approximation to the Langevin SDE.

Remark: The dynamics of SGD is much more complicated than LD. The variance of the effective SGD noise Σ(θ) depends on position in the loss landscape. Moreover, at late time, SGD may never converge to a single stationary distribution.

In Section 4 we will study a neural network at large N (= width) trained with gradient flow (as an approximation to SGD). We will compare the qualitative results to training via Bayesian inference.

In Section 5 we will sketch a beautiful but technical example of Bayesian phase transitions in toy models of grokking (Rubin et al. 2024), comparing the results to observed grokking transitions in models trained with SGD/Adam.

For yet another comparison of Bayesian vs. SGD/Adam phase transitions in toy models of superposition (Elhage et al. 2022), incorporating the methods of singular learning theory, see (Chen et al. 2023).

Despite lots of qualitative and empirical similarities between Bayesian learning and actual SGD/Adam training, the precise theoretical details relating the two remain elusive. It is an interesting open problem to form a more direct connection.

2.6 Comparison with QFT

This short subsection is a translation guide, aimed mainly at readers arriving from high-energy or condensed-matter physics — if the words "action" and "path integral" mean more to you than "posterior" and "marginal likelihood," read on; everyone else may safely skip ahead.

Nearly everything in these notes lives, in the first instance, in Euclidean equilibrium statistical mechanics: probability distributions of Boltzmann–Gibbs form P∝e−βE, partition functions, free energies. For a field theorist, a partition function with sources,

Z[J]=∫Dϕe−S[ϕ]+∫Jϕ,

is a moment generating functional; its logarithm generates connected correlation functions (cumulants); the action S encodes the microscopic rules of the system, and a quadratic action means a free (Gaussian) theory, with everything else treated by perturbing around it. In these notes the role of the field ϕ is played variously by the weights θ of a network, by an order parameter such as the overlap R of Section 2.2, or — most usefully — by the network function f(x) itself, with the input x playing the role of the spacetime coordinate. Functional integrals over the network function are developed carefully in Sections 3.3 and 3.5, and the reader coming from QFT will find many familiar ingredients there dressed up as learning theory: Wick's theorem, sources, cumulants, effective actions.

If your instincts were trained on Lorentzian signature, picture everything here as already Wick-rotated. There is no i/ℏ: the weights e−S are real and positive, as after the standard continuation

ZQFT​=∫Dϕeℏi​S[ϕ]τ=it​ZE​=∫Dϕe−SE​[ϕ]/ℏ.

The role of ℏ — the parameter controlling the size of fluctuations around saddle points — is played here by temperature, or by 1/N at large width, or by 1/n at large sample size.

When we eventually study the dynamics of training as a field theory in Section 6, a genuinely real-time formalism does appear — a path integral over trajectories with a causal structure and a response field. That's the closest object in these notes to a Lorentzian field theory, and is precisely the Martin–Siggia–Rose construction of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

For readers who would like physics references alongside the learning-theory ones: David Tong's lecture notes (Tong 2012; Tong 2012; Tong 2012; Tong 2006) are a friendly introduction to statistical physics, statistical field theory, kinetic theory, and QFT respectively; Lancaster and Blundell (Lancaster & Blundell 2014) is a gentle conceptual route into QFT; Altland and Simons (Altland & Simons 2010) bridges toward condensed-matter field theory (and contains the Langevin/MSRJD material used in Section 6); Pathria (Pathria & Beale 2011) is a standard graduate statistical mechanics text; Goldenfeld (Goldenfeld 2018) is the classic on phase transitions and the renormalization group; and Zinn-Justin (Zinn-Justin 2002) is the encyclopedic reference for the functional formalism.

3. Large width at initialization: the Gaussian process limit

The next few sections are all about different limits in neural networks, in which some parameter(s) become large. Such limits are where physical/statistical analyses really shine. Studying them teaches some basic lessons about how we should (and should not) initialize networks, and how to choose other hyperparameters. It also leads to analytically solvable models that display many properties we see in practice: lazy vs. rich learning, double descent, phase transitions, scaling laws for optimal learning. For further pedagogical references on much of this material, we recommend (Roberts et al. 2022; Spiliopoulos et al. 2025; Ringel et al. 2025) and the online lectures (Hanin 2026).

We'll begin in this section with a classic result (Neal 1996; Lee et al. 2018; Yang 2019; Hanin 2023) about increasing the width of a network at fixed depth and training-sample size.

Modern neural networks are more sophisticated than the simple MLP's discussed here, but they share many of the same features. Layer norms solve the problem of trainability at large depth, but the analysis of rich/lazy regimes, feature learning, and hyperparameter scaling is still relevant. See e.g. the discussion of μP in Section 5.5.

3.1 Notation

We'll use the following notation for neural networks and training data.

  • θ∈RP trainable network parameters (weights, biases)
  • (xμ,yμ)μ=1n​ training data samples, with xμ∈Rd and yμ∈R (unless otherwise stated)
  • fθ​:Rd→R network function

For MLP's in particular (also called FCN's = fully connected networks)

  • {zi(ℓ)​}i=1Nℓ​​ pre-activations in layer ℓ∈{0,...,L+1}
  • L= number of hidden layers (depth); Nℓ​= width of ℓ'th layer; N0​=d and NL+1​=1. We will often take constant hidden depth, N1​=...=NL​=N.
  • ϕ:R→R activation function (assumed the same in all layers except the first)
  • network recursion zi(ℓ)​=⎩⎨⎧​∑j=1Nℓ−1​​wij(ℓ)​ϕ(zj(ℓ−1)​)+bi(ℓ)​∑j=1d​wij(1)​xj​+bi(1)​​ℓ≥2ℓ=1​ with z(0)=x and z(L+1)=f; parameters are θ={w(ℓ),b(ℓ)}ℓ=1L+1​ .

3.2 Choosing parameter variances

Consider a fully connected network of depth L with layer widths Nℓ​ as in Section 3.1. Suppose we keep L fixed but make the Nℓ​ very large. Suppose also that the network is initialized randomly, with all weights and biases chosen from normal distributions

wij(ℓ)​∼N(0,σw(ℓ)​),bi(ℓ)​∼N(0,σb(ℓ)​).

One would like the variances of activations to stay roughly constant from layer to layer, as the Nℓ​ get large. From

zi(ℓ)​=wi(ℓ)​⋅ϕ(z(ℓ−1))+bi(ℓ)​

(where we've written wi​=(wi,1​,...,wi,Nℓ−1​​) and z(ℓ−1)=(z1(ℓ−1)​,...,zNℓ−1​(ℓ−1)​) as vectors) we get

Var(zi(ℓ)​)​=j=1∑Nℓ−1​​Var(wij(ℓ)​)E[ϕ(zj(ℓ−1)​)2]+Var(bi(ℓ)​)=σw(ℓ)​j=1∑Nℓ−1​​(Var(ϕ(zj(ℓ−1)​))+E[ϕ(zj(ℓ−1)​)]2)+σb(ℓ)​.​

Here we've conditioned on the previous layer, and used that for independent mean-zero X and arbitrary Y, Var(XY)=Var(X)E[Y2], along with additivity of variance for independent summands. We expect the quantity in parentheses, which involves only the activation function and the order-one previous-layer preactivations, to remain of order 1 as Nℓ​→∞. (We'll sharpen this estimate in Section 3.7.) Thus

Var(zi(ℓ)​)≈Nℓ−1​σw(ℓ)​+σb(ℓ)​,

implying that in order to maintain order-1 preactivations we should initialize with

σw(ℓ)​≈Nℓ−1​1​asNℓ−1​→∞.

and σb(ℓ)​ small enough that it doesn't interfere. The initialization (3.5) is called "fan-in" initialization, and goes back to LeCun and collaborators in the 90's (LeCun et al. 1998).

3.3 Gaussian processes

A Gaussian process f:Rm→R with mean function μ and covariance kernel K is a random function such that on any p inputs (x1,...,xp)∈(Rm)p the vector of function values is Gaussian

​f(x1)⋮f(xp)​​∼N​​μ(x1)⋮μ(xp)​​,​K(x1,x1)⋮K(xp,x1)​⋯⋱⋯​K(x1,xp)⋮K(xp,xp)​​​.

Here μ:Rm→R and K:Rm×Rm→R are fixed, deterministic functions that control the mean and covariance of any tuple of values of f. The function K, often called the kernel of the process, is symmetric: K(x,x′)=K(x′,x).

Let `dx' denote a measure on Rm (it need not be the usual Lebesgue measure). If K, as integral kernel, has an inverse K−1 satisfying

∫dx′K−1(x,x′)K(x′,x′′)=δ(x−x′′)

then there's also a "physics definition" of a Gaussian process. It's not entirely rigorous, as it invokes multi-dimensional functional integrals. Mathematically, it's best thought of as a heuristic tool, which comes with a package of axiomatic manipulations whose actual results can (and should) all be fully justified by other means. The manipulations are all quite intuitive, though, and familiar to quantum field theorists, so we mention this formalism here. The idea is that, just like a single Gaussian variable `z' has a probability measure

P(z)=Z1​e−21​K−1(z−μ)2,Z=∫dze−21​K−1(z−μ)2=2πK​,

a Gaussian process f has a (non-rigorous) measure

P[f]Z​=Z1​e−21​∫dxdx′(f(x)−μ(x))K−1(x,x′)(f(x′)−μ(x′)),‘=’∫Dfe−21​∫dxdx′(f(x)−μ(x))K−1(x,x′)(f(x′)−μ(x′)).​

If the kernel and the measure theory on the input space Rm are nice enough to allow K to be diagonalized, with a discrete basis of orthonormal eigenfunctions {ϕk​(x)}k=1∞​ and eigenvalues λ1​≥λ2​≥…>0 (so that K−1 has eigenvalues 1/λk​), then P[f] can be understood as an infinite-dimensional Gaussian. Writing f(x)−μ(x)=∑k=1∞​ak​ϕk​(x),

P[f]=Z1​e−21​∑k=1∞​ak2​/λk​,Z=k=1∏∞​(2πλk​)1/2.

One virtue of the physics formalism is that it organizes expectation values of products of f(x)'s. Let μ=0 for simplicity (to generalize to any μ, just shift f↦f−μ below). Let J:Rm→R be an arbitrary (nice...) function and define

Z[J]=∫Dfe−21​∫dxdx′f(x)K−1(x,x′)f(x′)+∫dxJ(x)f(x).

The integral evaluates formally to

Z[J]=Z[0]⋅e21​∫dxdx′J(x)K(x,x′)J(x′).

Then expectation values can be expressed via derivatives, which by (3.12) become

E[f(x1)...f(xp)]​=Z[0]1​δJ(x1)δ​...δJ(xp)δ​Z[J]​J=0​=pairs{i1​,i2​}∪...∪{ip−1​,ip​}={1,2,...,p}∑​j=1∏p/2​K(xi2j−1​,xi2j​).​

The sum is over partitions of {1,...,p} into pairs, and vanishes if p is odd. Eqn. (3.14) is called Wick's Theorem in QFT, Isserlis's Theorem in probability (and it's correct, despite the non-rigorous derivation here).

Exercise 3.1 (Wick's theorem). If you haven't seen this before, derive (3.12) by completing the square in (3.11), and then derive (3.14) by differentiating. Check the first two cases explicitly: E[f(x1)f(x2)]=K(x1,x2), and E[f(x1)f(x2)f(x3)f(x4)]=K12K34+K13K24+K14K23 (with Kij=K(xi,xj)). How many terms appear at p=6?

Solution

Complete the square: shifting f→f+KJ (schematically, f(x)→f(x)+∫dx′K(x,x′)J(x′)) decouples the source, leaving Z[J]=Z[0]e21​∫JKJ. Each derivative δ/δJ(xi) acting on the exponential either brings down a factor ∫K(xi,⋅)J (which must later be hit by another derivative, else it dies at J=0) or closes a pair by hitting a previously produced factor, contributing K(xi,xj). Every surviving term therefore corresponds to a perfect pairing of {1,…,p}. For p=2 this gives K(x1,x2); for p=4, the three pairings K12K34+K13K24+K14K23; for p=6 there are 5!!=15 terms; in general (p−1)!!.

Another virtue of the physics formalism is that it neatly connects higher cumulants to deviations from Gaussianity. In general, the p-th cumulant κp​(X1​,...,Xp​) of random variables X1​,...,Xp​ is defined recursively via

E(X1​⋯Xp​)=partition Π of {1,...,p}∑​blocks {i1​,...,ik​}⊂Π∏​κk​(Xi1​​,...,Xik​​)

For example, κ1​(X)=E(X), κ2​(X1​,X2​)=Cov(X1​,X2​)=E(X1​X2​)−E(X1​)E(X2​). In physics, the κp​'s are called connected correlation functions; they measure the part of a joint expectation that's not captured by expectations of subsets of the variables involved. For a Gaussian process,

κ2​(f(x1),f(x2))=K(x1,x2);κp​(f(x1),...,f(xp))=0for all p>2,

as can easily be seen directly from (3.14), where joint expectations for p>2 all factor into products of pairs. Thus, nonvanishing higher κp​'s are a measure of non-Gaussianity.

This appears in the functional-integral formalism as follows. Suppose that f:Rm→R is a random function that's governed by a functional probability distribution

P[f]=Z1​e−S[f],

for some functional S:{functions f}→R. (In physics S is called the action.) Then just as in (3.11), we can introduce the generating function

Z[J]:=∫Dfe−S[f]+∫dxJ(x)f(x)⇒E[f(x1)...f(xp)]=Z[0]1​δJ(x1)δ​...δJ(xp)δ​Z[J]​J=0​

The cumulants appear naturally as derivatives of logZ[J], otherwise known as the (sourced) free energy:

κp​(f(x1),...,f(xp))=δJ(x1)δ​...δJ(xp)δ​logZ[J]​J=0​,

which in turn means (formally) that

Z[J]=expp=1∑∞​p!1​∫dx1...dxpκp​(f(x1),...,f(xp))J(x1)...J(xp),

a generating function of cumulants. The original S[f] is the inverse Legendre transform of logZ[J] (by definition of Z[J]). Expanded as a formal series in the cumulants (assuming they are small), and assuming E[f(x)]=0 for simplicity, it takes the form

S[f]=​21​∫dx1dx2κ2−1​(x1,x2)f(x1)f(x2)−∫dx1dx2dx3dy1dy2dy3κ2−1​(x1,y1)κ2−1​(x2,y2)κ2−1​(x3,y3)κ3​(y1,y2,y3)f(x1)f(x2)f(x3)−∫dx1dx2dx3dx4(κ2−1​)4[κ4​−κ3​κ2−1​κ3​terms]f(x1)f(x2)f(x3)f(x4)−…​

Physicists might recognize this as a sum of Feynman diagrams, with cumulants giving the vertices. A key structure is that the p-th order term in the effective action contains only κp​ and lower cumulants. In particular, f is a Gaussian process if and only if S[f] is quadratic; and small deviations from Gaussianity, measured by cumulants, provide the higher-order terms in S[f].

3.4 The NNGP correspondence

A classic result in the theory of neural networks is that, at fixed depth and large width, with weight covariances scaled as in Section 3.2, the network function at initialization converges to a Gaussian process. The theorem appeared in the 90's (Neal 1996) for a single hidden layer, and was generalized more recently to deeper networks and different architectures, cf. (Lee et al. 2018; Yang 2019; Hanin 2023).

In this theorem, the source of stochasticity in the network function comes from the random initializations of network parameters. One can think of randomly initializing a swarm of networks and asking what sorts of values the network function outputs. The result is significant because of its universality, and because it feeds into (and greatly simplifies) further analyses of training.

The derivation proceeds via induction. We'll just sketch it here, for MLP's.

2

For simplicity we'll assume that biases have been set to zero. We'll take the weight variances to be σw(ℓ)​=σw​/Nℓ−1​ as in Section 3.2, for some fixed constant σw​.

In the first network layer, the preactivations are

zi(1)​(x)=j=1∑d​wij(1)​xj​,wij(1)​∼N(0,σw​/d).

At fixed x, each zi(1)​(x) is a sum of d i.i.d. Gaussian variables (with coefficients xj​), and thus is Gaussian itself, with E[zi(1)​]=0 and

Cov(zi(1)​(x),zi(1)​(x′))=j,j′=1∑d​δjj′​σw​/dCov(wij​,wij′​)​​xj​xj′′​=σw​dx⋅x′​,

thus zi(1)​ is a Gaussian process (GP) with

zi(1)​∼N(0,K(1)),K(1)(x,x′)=σw​dx⋅x′​.

In the second layer, we've got

zi(2)​=j=1∑N1​​wij(2)​ϕ(zj(1)​),wij(2)​∼N(0,σw​/N1​).

If we condition on the preactivations of the first layer, the same argument gives

zi(2)​∼N(0,K(2)),K(2)(z(1),z(1)′)=σw​N1​ϕ(z(1))⋅ϕ(z(1)′)​.

Thus we again get a Gaussian process. The problem is that if we don't condition on the preactivations, the kernel of this GP is not deterministic, but becomes a random variable itself: ϕ(z(1))⋅ϕ(z(1)′). This is where the infinite-width limit comes in. Heuristically, the central limit theorem implies that the sum of products of (non-Gaussian!) random variables on the LHS of (3.26) will become Gaussian as N1​→∞. More concretely, we can calculate and bound the variance

Var(K(2)(z(1),z(1)′))​=N12​σw2​​Var(ϕ(z(1))⋅ϕ(z(1)′))=N12​σw2​​N1​⋅Var(ϕ(z1(1)​)ϕ(z1(1)​′))→0as N1​→∞​

as long as the first-layer preactivations are order one (independent of N1​), and the activation function is reasonable (any standard choice will be). Thus, as N1​→∞, we can replace the stochastic kernel K(2) by its expectation,

Kˉ(2)(x,x′):=σw​Ez1(1)​(x),z1(1)​(x′)∼N(0,K(1))​[ϕ(z1(1)​(x))ϕ(z1(1)​(x′))]

Each subsequent layer is the same. At infinite width, the kernels become deterministic, and obey a recursion

Kˉ(ℓ)(x,x′)=σw​Eu(x),u(x′)∼N(0,Kˉ(ℓ−1))​[ϕ(u(x))ϕ(u(x′))],

with KˉL+1(x,x′) ultimately governing a GP for the network function f(x).

Remark (exact kernels): For a few special activation functions, the Gaussian expectation in (3.31) can be evaluated in closed form, giving explicit NNGP kernels. Write K11​=Kˉ(ℓ−1)(x,x), K22​=Kˉ(ℓ−1)(x′,x′) and K12​=Kˉ(ℓ−1)(x,x′) for the previous layer's kernel values. For ReLU, ϕ(u)=max(u,0), one finds the arc-cosine kernel of Cho and Saul (Cho & Saul 2009),

Kˉ(ℓ)(x,x′)=2πσw​​K11​K22​​(sinϑ+(π−ϑ)cosϑ),cosϑ=K11​K22​​K12​​,

and for the sigmoid-like activation ϕ=erf Williams (Williams 1997) found

Kˉ(ℓ)(x,x′)=π2σw​​arcsin((1+2K11​)(1+2K22​)​2K12​​).

Iterating either formula through the layers gives the exact infinite-width kernel of a deep ReLU or erf network in a few lines of code. (Deriving (3.32)–(3.33) is a pleasant but somewhat lengthy Gaussian-integral workout.)

Exercise 3.2 (The NNGP correspondence, empirically (lab)). Fix two unit-norm inputs x,x′∈Rd with, say, d=8 and x⋅x′=0.5. For widths N∈{3,30,300}, sample M=104 independent initializations of the one-hidden-layer erf network f(x)=∑i=1N​ci​erf(ai​⋅x) with fan-in variances (σw​=1). (a) Make a histogram of the values f(x) across the ensemble, and overlay the Gaussian density with the variance Kˉ(2)(x,x) predicted by (3.33); watch the visibly non-Gaussian N=3 histogram converge. (b) Make a scatter plot of the pairs (f(x),f(x′)) and compare the sample 2×2 covariance with the predicted kernel matrix. (c) For each initialization, record the stochastic kernel K(2) of (3.27), and verify that its variance across initializations decays like 1/N (that's the mechanism by which the kernel becomes deterministic).

Solution

Everything is closed-form thanks to the erf kernel (3.33), which is the point of choosing erf. Expected observations: (a) at N=3 the histogram has visibly heavy tails and excess kurtosis (the output is a sum of only three i.i.d. non-Gaussian terms); at N=30 deviations are still detectable; at N=300 the histogram is indistinguishable from the predicted Gaussian at this sample size. (b) The sample covariance matches the 2×2 kernel matrix built from (3.33) to within the Monte Carlo error O(M−1/2). (c) A log–log plot of Var(K(2)) against N has slope −1, as in the variance computation of Section 3.4. The whole lab is ∼20 lines of NumPy; the one subtlety is to histogram over initializations at fixed inputs, not over inputs.

3.5 NNGP via functional integrals

One can also analyze large width at initialization via functional integrals. This just reorganizes the above steps. We'll illustrate how it works for a network with one hidden layer and zero biases, N2​=1,N1​=N,N0​=d,

f(x)=i=1∑N​ci​ϕ(ai​⋅x),ci​∈R,ai​,x∈Rd.

The initial distribution of weights, with fan-in variances, is

P(c,a)=Z1​e−2σw​N​∣c∣2−2σw​d​∣a∣2.

To push this forward to a distribution on the first-layer preactivations zi​=ai​⋅x, we integrate against a delta function:

P(c,z)=∫daP(c,a)i∏​δ(zi​(x)−ai​⋅x).

Here the zi​(x) are arbitrary functions of x, and are only tied to the network values ai​⋅x via δ(zi​(x)−ai​⋅x). Eqn. (3.36) represents a functional probability density on the functions zi​. To evaluate it, introduce a second set of "Lagrange multiplier" functions z~i​, and write

δ(zi​(x)−ai​⋅x)=∫Dz~i​ei∫dxz~i​(x)(zi​(x)−ai​⋅x),

and then do the exact Gaussian integral over a's, and then over z~'s:

P(c,z)​=Z1​∫daDz~e−2σw​N​∣c∣2−∑i​2σw​d​∣ai​∣2+i∑i​∫dxz~i​(x)(zi​(x)−ai​⋅x)=Z1​∫daDz~exp[−2σw​N​∣c∣2+∑i​[−2σw​d​(ai​+diσw​​∫dxz~i​(x)x)2−2dσw​​∫dxdx′z~i​(x)(x⋅x′)z~i​(x′)+i∫dxz~i​(x)zi​(x)]]=Z′1​∫Dz~e−2σw​N​∣c∣2−2dσw​​∑i​∫dxdx′z~i​(x)(x⋅x′)z~i​(x′)+i∑i​∫dxz~i​(x)zi​(x)]=Z′′1​e−2σw​N​∣c∣2−2σw​1​∑i​∫dxdx′zi​(x)(dx⋅x′​)−1zi​(x′).​

We clearly see the first-layer GP kernel K(1)(x,x′)=dσw​​x⋅x′ appearing.

To push-forward to the network outputs f=c⋅ϕ(z), we just do this again:

P(f)​=∫dcDzP(c,z)δ(f(x)−c⋅ϕ(z(x)))=Z′′1​∫dcDzDf~​e[−2σw​N​∣c∣2−2σw​1​∑i​∫dxdx′zi​(x)(dx⋅x′​)−1zi​(x′)+i∫dxf~​(x)(f(x)−c⋅ϕ(z(x)))]=Z′′′1​∫DzDf~​e[−2σw​1​∫dxdx′(dx⋅x′​)−1z(x)⋅z(x′)−2Nσw​​∫dxdx′f~​(x)[ϕ(z(x))⋅ϕ(z(x′))]f~​(x′)+i∫dxf~​(x)f(x)]​

The problem is that it's now impossible to do the integral over the z's exactly, because (for general activation function ϕ) the action is no longer quadratic in them. However, as N→∞, we can treat exp[−2Nσw​​∫dxdx′f~​(x)[ϕ(z(x))⋅ϕ(z(x′))]f~​(x′)] as a perturbation, and approximate the exponent [ϕ(z(x))⋅ϕ(z(x′))] by its expectation value under the Gaussian measure exp[−2σw​1​∫dxdx′(dx⋅x′​)−1z(x)⋅z(x′)] (with kernel K(1)) on the z's. To be clear, the approximation that's happening is of the form

EeN1​X=eN1​EX+O(Var(X)/N2)

Up to O(1/N) corrections, that produces the deterministic kernel Kˉ(2)(x,x′) = σw​Ezi​(x),zi​(x′)∼N(0,K(1)(x,x′))​ϕ(zi​(x))ϕ(zi​(x′)) from the previous section, and we get

P(f)​=Z′′′′1​∫Df~​e−21​∫dxdx′f~​(x)Kˉ(2)(x,x′)f~​(x′)+i∫dxf~​(x)f(x)+O(N1​)=Z′′′′′1​e−21​∫dxdx′f(x)Kˉ(2)(x,x′)−1f(x′)+O(N1​).​

3.6 L/N

The inductive argument of Section 3.4 does not hold at infinite L. There are two potential problems.

First, a factor of σw​ appears with every layer. These factors will accumulate, and can lead either to vanishing kernels (which also turns out to imply vanishing gradients during training), in which case the network will collapse; or to unbounded kernels (and increasingly large gradients), in which case the network will be chaotic and again untrainable. We'll revisit this in Section 3.7. With careful tuning, the issue can be avoided. For example, in a deep linear network (DLN) with ϕ(z)=z, one can just take σw​=1, known as LeCun initialization (LeCun et al. 1998). In a ReLU network, the correct choice instead is σw​=2, known as He initialization (He et al. 2015).

Even with σw​ tuned, according to the activation function, so that on average the GP kernels remain order-one from layer to layer, non-Gaussianities can still accumulate. The upshot is that it is not width alone, say of typical size N, but rather the ratio L/N of depth-to-width that controls the effective behavior of a network — including its departure from pure Gaussianity at large N.

This behavior is analyzed in Chapters 3-4 of (Roberts et al. 2022) using functional-integral methods. In particular, Chapter 3 considers the simple example of DLN's, and produces exact recursion relations for higher cumulants of preactivations in each layer. It is shown that in a network of constant hidden width N, the leading non-Gaussianity is

κ4(L+1)​=[(1+N2​)L−1](κ2(L+1)​)2=[(e2L/N−1)−N1​N2L​e2L/N+O(N−2)](κ2(L+1)​)2,

where the expansion on the RHS is at finite L/N and L,N→∞. For small L/N, the non-Gaussianity remains small but finite, of size L/N. For large L/N, κ4(L+1)​ blows up, as do all the other cumulants. The network outputs will fluctuate chaotically from one instantiation to another, and the network again becomes untrainable.

Here's a more direct analysis, in a special case, following (Hanin 2026, Lecture 2). Consider a DLN of length L with input and hidden layers all of width N:

zℓ=wℓz(ℓ−1),z(0)=x,f(x)=z(L+1)=w(L+1)⋯w(1)x,

initialized so that wij(ℓ)​∼N(0,1/N). Conditional on z(ℓ−1), the vector z(ℓ) is Gaussian z(ℓ)∼N(0,N1​IN​∣z(ℓ−1)∣2), so its norm satisfies the recursion

∣z(ℓ)∣2∼∣z(ℓ−1)∣2NχN2​​.

(Recall that χN2​ is the distribution of the sum of squares of N i.i.d. standard Gaussian variables.) Let's normalize the input so that ∣x∣=1. Then the recursion implies that

∣f(x)∣2=dk=1∏L+1​NχN2​​=expk=1∑L+1​(logχN2​−logN),

with each factor of χN2​ independent. At large N, we have logχN2​−logN=N(−N1​,N2​)+O(N21​), so at large N,L with L/N fixed

∣f(x)∣2=deN(−NL​,2NL​),

up to higher O(N21​ corrections. Thus, as L/N grows, the expectation of E∣f(x)∣→0 but the variance and higher cumulants blow up.

The lesson once again is

  • N→∞, L/N=0: Gaussian process, no correlations across layers (and as we'll see in the next section, no "feature learning").
  • N,L→∞, L/N small: controlled correlations, trainable network (and, as we'll see, feature learning during training). In open-weight LLM's today, L/N≈0.005–0.01; see Exercise 3.3.
  • N,L→∞, L/N large: chaotic and untrainable.

Exercise 3.3 (Depth-to-width ratios in the wild). Look up the depth L (number of transformer blocks) and the width N (model/embedding dimension) for a few families of open-weight language models — e.g. GPT-2, the Llama family, the Qwen family — and compute L/N for each. How much does the ratio vary across families, across sizes within a family, and across the years? Is everyone training in the "controlled correlations" window?

Solution

Representative numbers at the time of writing (take the width N to be the model/embedding dimension): GPT-2 small has L/N=12/768≈0.016 and GPT-2 XL 48/1600=0.030; Llama-2-7B has 32/4096≈0.008; Llama-2-70B, 80/8192≈0.010; Llama-3-405B, 126/16384≈0.008. The striking finding is how stable the ratio is: modern open-weight families cluster around L/N∼0.005–0.01 across two orders of magnitude in parameter count, comfortably inside the "controlled correlations" window, with the earliest (GPT-2-era) models running noticeably deeper for their width. Whether this stability reflects tuned wisdom or copied convention is a fair discussion question.

3.7 Edge of chaos

We briefly remark that the analysis of how to tune initialization variances σw​,σb​ (etc.) leading to stable network behavior over a large number of layers (the first point in Section 3.6) is sometimes called finding the "edge of chaos."

The term dates back to dynamical systems theory from the 80's and 90's, referring to the boundary between ordered and chaotic phases. It was adapted to neural networks around 2016 (Poole et al. 2016; Schoenholz et al. 2017). The idea was to treat the progression through layers of a network as a dynamical system, and to ask: given two nearby inputs x,x′, for what range of hyperparameters (σw​,σb​, etc.) and to what depth do they remain nearby, without either a) collapsing; or (b) blowing up chaotically (with no correlation). The analysis roughly amounts to making sure the kernel recursion of (3.27), (3.31) leads to kernels that neither collapse nor blow up. Doing it carefully, theoretically, can produce elementary trainable networks (with no layer norms!) over 10,000 layers deep (Xiao et al. 2018).

For MLP's with ReLu activations, the edge of chaos is just the one point σw​=2,σb​=0. Moving slightly away from this point, one can estimate the "critical depth" Lc​ at which the network either collapses or blows up – see (Schoenholz et al. 2017). For MLP's with other activation functions, the edge of chaos is more interesting. For ϕ=tanh, the phase diagram is shown in Figure 4.

The quantity `χ1​' that controls the critical depth (Lc​=−1/logχ1​) is the derivative of the layer-to-layer kernel recursion at its fixed point, which measures how fast nearby inputs separate. Importantly, the same quantity χ1​ also controls the size of gradients as they back-prop through a network during training. There's a direct link between behavior at initialization and behavior during training. We come to training next.

4. The NTK and large width during training

In this section, we consider training networks that are randomly initialized as in Section 3.2, and their behavior at large width. The lesson will be that as width→∞ these networks effectively behave like linear models: their parameters θ never stray far from their values θ0​ at initialization, hence

fθ​(x)≈fθlin​(x):=fθ0​​(x)+(θ−θ0​)⋅∇θ​fθ0​​(x).

Under suitable conditions, the network itself also converges exponentially fast to a "memorizing network" that fits the training data perfectly. Heuristically, this happens because small changes in many parameters, as in (4.1), can add up to an order-one change in the network values themselves. Nevertheless, the network never experiences phase transitions or feature learning — we'll make this more precise below. The large-width regime (at finite depth and training data) is thus known as the lazy regime, or the NTK regime.

Although this regime does not describe the feature learning that makes practical networks interesting, it is important to understand for at least two reasons: it is an honest, analytically solvable model of training; and it is a precise lesson in what must be avoided if one wants genuine feature learning — a lesson we act on in Section 5.

We also emphasize the connection between Section 3 and the current analysis. Both involve the same large-width limit. At initialization, it leads to a Gaussian process. During training, we'll see that it leads to a linear model with lazy learning, converging once again to a GP at late training times.

4.1 Gradient flow and the NTK

Throughout this section, we approximate SGD with continuous-time gradient flow (cf. Section 2.5). This involves two approximations. First we update on the entire training dataset {(xμ,yμ)}μ=1n​ at each step, rather than on batches, so that SGD becomes GD:

θk+1​−θk​=−ηGD​∇θ​Lθ​({xμ,yμ})​θ=θk​​

where

Lθ​=Lθ​({xμ,yμ}):=μ=1∑n​ℓθ​(xμ,yμ)

is the full empirical loss.

Second, we scale down the learning rate ηGD​=λ−1η and scale up the number of training steps, setting k=⌊λt] where t≥0 is a continuous "time" variable. As λ→∞, the gradient descent converges to a gradient flow

θ˙:=dtd​θ=−η∇θ​Lθ​.

All theorems in this section can be extended to SGD, adding additional error terms to bound the difference between SGD and GF. (See for example (Spiliopoulos et al. 2025, Chapter 19).)

4.1.1 Geometry of gradient flows

Suppose that X is a smooth Riemannian manifold, with nondegenerate metric g=gab​dxadxb, inverse metric g−1=gab∂xa∂​∂xb∂​, and a function h:X→R. Then one can define gradient flow with respect to (h,g) as

x˙a(t)=−ηgab∂xb∂h​,or abstractly:x˙=−ηg−1(dh).

Note that this equation does not make sense (it's not coordinate-free) without an inverse-metric (a bilinear form on each cotangent space T∗X). The inverse-metric is used to relate the differential dh=(∂b​h)b=1dimX​ on the RHS to a vector field g−1dh, which is the right sort of geometric object to induce a flow on X.

In neural networks, X=RP is the space of parameters θ and h=L is the loss function. One always assumes a constant Euclidean metric in parameter space g=∑i=1P​(dθi)2=δij​dθidθj, in order to define SGD/GD/GF/etc. This is the source of some of the simplest inductive biases of trained models, and also why one expects "features" to have some linear structure. Eqn. (4.5) with the metric looks like

θ˙i=−ηδij∂j​Lθ​.

Now return to the general setting of Riemannian manifolds. Suppose we have a smooth map f:X→Y between two manifolds, and moreover that h:X→R is the pull-back of a function hY:Y→R, meaning h(x)=hY(f(x)). Let {fα}α=1dimY​ be the components of the map f, in local coordinates yα on Y. Then the inverse-metric on X induces an inverse-metric on Y (called its push-forward):

f∗​(g−1)=f∗​[gab∂xa∂​∂xb∂​]=gαβgab∂xa∂fα​∂xb∂fβ​​​∂yα∂​∂yβ∂​.

Schematically, gαβ=(Jg−1JT), where Jαa​=∂xa∂fα​ is the Jacobian matrix of f. Then the gradient flow on X induces a gradient flow on Y, given by

y˙​α=−ηgαβ∂yβ∂hY​.

Let's apply this to neural networks, where f:RP→Rn is the function from parameters to network outputs on the training data (xμ,yμ), i.e. fμ(θ)=fθ​(xμ) in our standard notation. The loss function is indeed a pullback of a function on Rn, since it depends on parameters θ only through the network values on training data,

Lθ​=L(f)(f(θ)),L(f)(f):=μ=1∑n​ℓ(fμ,yμ).

The push-forward of the gradient flow in parameter space becomes

dtd​fμ=−ηΘμν∂fν∂L(f)​,Θμν=(Jδ−1JT)μν=i=1∑P​∂θi∂fθ​(xμ)​∂θi∂fθ​(xν)​.

The inverse-metric Θμν on the space of function values is called the "neural tangent kernel" or NTK. The name was coined in (Jacot et al. 2018); it also appeared in (Du et al. 2019) under a different name. Here we are emphasizing that it's a completely natural geometric object, for any neural network (in fact, for any ML model).

We mention one final bit of geometry. Let δμν​ be a standard Euclidean metric in the space of function values, with inverse δμν. The gradient of the loss δμν∂L(f)/∂fν that appears in (4.10) (contracted with an inverse metric) is sometimes called the residual, and denoted Δμ or rμ. For MSE loss, we've got L(f)=21​∑μ=1n​(fμ−yμ)2=δμν​(fμ−yμ)(fν−yν). Then the residual is just the difference between function values and truth for the training data:

Δμ:=δμν∂L(f)/∂fν=fμ−yμ.

Noting that yμ are constants, the gradient-flow equation can be recast as

dtd​Δμ=−ηΘμν​Θμρδρν​​​Δν.

Those who have studied gauge theory may recognize this as an equation for parallel transport, with respect to an n×n matrix-valued connection ηΘμν​. If one knows the dependence of Θ on time (which in general is far from trivial — see the exercise below) the solution is a time-ordered exponential

Δμ(t)=(Pexp[−η∫Θ(t)dt])νμ​Δν(0).

Exercise 4.1 (The NTK from the chain rule). Derive the flow equation (4.10) for the function values fμ directly, using only the chain rule — no geometry required. (The geometric derivation explains why an object like Θμν had to appear; the chain rule shows it appears in three lines.)

Solution

By the chain rule and the gradient-flow equation,

dtd​fμ=∇θ​fμ⋅θ˙=−η∇θ​fμ⋅∇θ​L=−η∇θ​fμ⋅ν∑​∇θ​fν∂fν∂L(f)​=−ηΘμν∂fν∂L(f)​,

using in the middle step that L depends on θ only through the function values fν.

Exercise 4.2 (How fast does the kernel move?). Show that the time derivative of the NTK satisfies

dtd​Θμν=−η[∇θ​fμ⋅∇θ2​fν⋅∇θ​fρ]∂fρ∂L(f)​+(μ↔ν),

where ∇θ2​fν=∇θ2​fθ​(xν) is the Hessian. Bounding the Hessian ultimately leads to the constant-NTK theorem in Section 4.3 below.

Solution

Differentiate Θμν=∇θ​fμ⋅∇θ​fν along the flow: dtd​Θμν=θ˙⋅∇θ2​fμ⋅∇θ​fν+∇θ​fμ⋅∇θ2​fν⋅θ˙. Substituting θ˙=−η∇θ​fρ∂L(f)/∂fρ gives the stated formula. Taking operator norms, ∥Θ˙∥≲η∥∇θ2​f∥∥∇θ​f∥2∣∂L/∂f∣∼η∥∇θ2​f∥∥Θ∥∣Δ∣: the kernel can only move as fast as the Hessian of the network function (not of the loss) allows — which is why bounding that Hessian at large width freezes the kernel.

4.2 Features

The Jacobian matrix Jμi​=∂fμ/∂θi measures how function values on the training data depend on small variations of the network weights. Assuming there are more parameters than training data, its singular value decomposition looks like

J=USVT,S=[diag(s1​,...,sn​)0n×(P−n)​].

The right singular vectors (columns of V) define natural modes in parameter space, while the left singular vectors (columns of U) are the natural modes in function-value space — where "natural" means with respect to how network outputs depend on weights. The n left singular vectors (together with their singular values si​) can be thought of, abstractly, as the features that a network has learned. A common definition of feature learning is that these singular vectors+values change during training.

The analysis of features can equivalently be performed via the NTK. As a matrix, we've got

Θ=JJT=US2UT,

with eigenvectors = the feature vectors, and eigenvalues = {si2​} . Thus feature learning happens when the NTK changes during training.

Remark: A closely related "dual" object that appears in other parts of learning theory is the Fisher information metric on parameter space RP. Its empirical version is

F:=JTJ=f∗(δ),

the pull-back (via the network function) of constant Euclidean metric on the space of function values on the training data. In coordinates, Fij​=∂θi∂fμ​δμν​∂θj∂fμ​.

The Fisher metric has eigenvalues (s12​,...,sn2​,0,...,0​P−n​), and is automatically degenerate when P>n (more parameters than training data points). This is one of the starting points of singular learning theory.

4.3 Constant NTK at large width

Now we get to the main theoretical result and simplification of this section.
