Suppose we've got an MLP of fixed depth L, and fixed training data size n, and take the width of all hidden layers to infinity. We'll assume the hidden widths all scale in a similar way NL​,NL−1​,...,N1​≈N→∞, and we initialize the network the standard way from Section 3.2. We want to show that for almost all samples of training data,

  • The NTK Θμν remains constant throughout training, up to O(1/N) corrections.
  • The networks itself linearizes: at any training time t, fθ(t)​(x)=fθ0​​(x)+(θ(t)−θ0​)⋅∇θ​fθ0​​(x)

A rigorous derivation is somewhat technical, and we refer the reader to (Du et al. 2019; Jacot et al. 2018), (Roberts et al. 2022, Ch. 11), (Spiliopoulos et al. 2025, Ch. 20) for complete arguments, explained from a variety of different perspectives. We'll just sketch the key ideas behind the result. See also (Hanin 2026, Lecture 3).

We'll simplify life by setting biases to zero, so the network becomes

fθ​(x)=z(L+1)(x),zi(ℓ)​=j∑​wij(ℓ)​ϕ(zj(ℓ−1)​).

First, we note that in order for NTK itself not to blow up at large width, we must rescale the learning rate:

η=Nη~​​,

with η~​ constant as N→∞. To see this, observe that the components of the gradient of the network function are

∇θ​f=(∇w(L+1)​f,∇w(L)​f,…,∇w1​f), ∇wℓ​f=Nℓ​×1[w(L+1)⋅ϕ′(z(L))⋅w(L)⋅ϕ′(z(L−1))⋯w(ℓ+1)⋅ϕ′(z(ℓ))]T​​1×Nℓ−1​[ϕ(z(ℓ−1))]T​​,

where we view the second factor as an Nℓ−1​-dimensional column vector, and the first factor as an Nℓ​-dimensional row vector, composed by multiplying weight matrices and the diagonal matrices ϕ′(z(ℓ′)):=diag(ϕ′(z1(ℓ′)​),...,ϕ′(zNℓ′​(ℓ′)​)) . The dimensions on the RHS match that of the Nℓ​×Nℓ−1​ matrix wℓ. Then the NTK looks like

Θμν​=ℓ=1∑L+1​∇wℓ​fμ⋅∇wℓ​fν=ℓ=1∑L+1​[(w(L+1)⋯ϕ′(z(ℓ)(xμ)))⋅(w(L+1)⋯ϕ′(z(ℓ)(xν)))][ϕ(z(ℓ−1)(xμ)⋅ϕ(z(ℓ−1)(xν))]​

At initialization and at large width, the factors in this formula coming from different layers all become independent, just like in the Gaussian process recursion of Section 3.4. We recognize E[ϕ(z(ℓ−1)(xμ)⋅ϕ(z(ℓ−1)(xν))]=σw​Nℓ−1​​Kˉ(ℓ)(xμ,xν) as Nℓ−1​ copies of the Gaussian process kernel from (3.31), which is of order one. (The expectation is taken over the random initialization parameters.) Similarly, define

Kˉ˙μν(ℓ)​=Kˉ˙(ℓ)(xμ,xν):=E[ϕ′(zi(ℓ−1)​(xμ))ϕ′(zi(ℓ−1)​(xν))](for any fixed i),

which is also of order one as N→∞, for reasonable choices of activation function. Then a quick calculation shows

E[Θμν]=ℓ=1∑(L+1)​σwL−ℓ​Nℓ−1​Kˉ˙μν(L+1)​⋯Kˉ˙μν(ℓ+1)​Kˉμν(ℓ)​,

a sum of L+1 terms that is each of order N. Thus, at fixed L, Θμν itself is of order N. With the rescaled learning rate, the RHS of the flow equation

dtd​fμ=−η~​(NΘμν​)∂fν∂L(f)​

remains of order one.

Caution: for large data size n and/or large depth L, the learning rate would need to be further rescaled, e.g. setting η=η~​/(Nn​L​).

We've discovered that the NTK grows linearly with N. To see that it's approximately constant we consider its derivative, which by Exercise 4.2 is bounded by the operator norm of the Hessian

​dtd​Θ​≲η~​N1​∥∇θ2​f∥⋅∥Θ∥.

The Hessian is a very sparse matrix, and turns out to be of order one at large N. We'll sketch how this works for one hidden layer (L=1), with one-dimensional output, following (Hanin 2026, Lecture 3).

An L=1 network can be written as

fθ​(x)=i=1∑N1​​ci​f(ai​⋅x),ci​∈R,ai​∈Rd,

where we've split the weights into a sum over neurons in the hidden layers. The Hessian clearly splits into blocks, one per hidden neuron,

∇θ2​fθ​(x)=i=1⨁N1​​(∇θ2​f)i​,(∇θ2​f)i​=(0ϕ′(ai​⋅x)x​ϕ′(ai​⋅x)xTci​ϕ′′(ai​⋅x)xxT​).

The operator norm of ∇θ2​f (the absolute value of the largest eigenvalue) is the maximum of the operator norms of the blocks. Each block, though, is of fixed size (d+1)×(d+1), and (at least at initialization) only includes O(1) quantities. Thus

∥∇θ2​f∥=maxi=1,...,N1​​∥(∇θ2​f)i​∥=O(1)as N=N1​→∞

It's reasonable to expect that this bound continues to hold during training, and with a bit more work it can be proven (though we won't do it here). It also holds for networks of arbitrary fixed depth.

Now let's put the pieces together. By the mean value theorem, at training time t, Θ(t)−Θ(0)=t⋅Θ˙(tˉ) for some tˉ∈[0,t] . Thus

​NΘ(t)​−NΘ(0)​​≤Nt​∥Θ˙(tˉ)∥≲tη~​N∥∇θ​f(tˉ)∥​N∥Θ(tˉ)∥​=O(N1​)

as N→∞, and we find that at large width the O(1) quantity Θ/N becomes constant. Similarly, the parameters obey θ(t)−θ(0)=tθ˙(tˉ) for some tˉ∈[0,t], so

∣θ(t)−θ(0)∣2​=t2∣θ˙(tˉ)∣2=N2t2η~​2​​μ=1∑n​Δμ∇θ​fμ​2≤N2t2η~​2​∣Δ∣2∣∇θ​f∣2≤N2nt2η~​2​∣Δ∣2∥Θ∥=O(N1​),​

or ∣θ(t)−θ(0)∣=O(1/N​) . Finally, by Taylor's theorem with remainder, the network function itself obeys

fθ​(x)−fθ0​​(x)=∇θ​f(x)​θ0​​⋅(θ−θ0​)+21​(θ−θ0​)⋅∇θ2​f(x)​θˉ​⋅(θ−θ0​)

for some θˉ∈[θ0​,θ]. Setting θ=θ(t) and using (4.31), we bound the error by

​21​(θ−θ0​)⋅∇θ2​f(x)​θˉ​⋅(θ−θ0​)​2≤41​∥∇θ2​f∥∣θ−θ0​∣2=O(1)⋅O(N1​),

so the linear approximation becomes exact as N→∞ .

4.4 Lazy learning

When the NTK is constant during training — confusingly often called the NTK regime — a network undergoes what is known as "lazy learning." It is not learning features, since the eigenvalues sμ2​ and eigenvectors uμ​ of the NTK are (by construction) constant. Nevertheless, the network function converges to its training data exponentially fast: from (4.12) with constant Θ, we have

3

Δμ(t)=(e−ηtΘ)μν​Δν(0),

where we recall that Δμ(t)=fμ−yμ=fθ(t)​(xμ)−yμ. Writing the residuals in an eigenbasis for the NTK, Δ=Δ^μuμ​ we see that

Δ^μ(t)=e−ηtsμ2​Δ^μ(0).

Each feature is learned at a characteristic timescale t≈1/sμ2​ .

Exercise 4.3 (Lazy predictions on test points). Derive that on an arbitrary test point x, not necessarily part of the training data,

fθ(t)​(x)=fθ0​​(x)−Θ(x,xμ)Θμν−1​(11−e−ηtΘ)νρ​Δρ(0)

where Θ(x,xμ)=∇θ​f(x)⋅∇θ​f(xμ) is the NTK for a test-train pair (which remains constant during training, just like the train-train NTK Θμν).

Solution

In the linearized regime, fθ(t)​(x)=fθ0​​(x)+∇θ​f(x)⋅(θ(t)−θ0​) with all gradients at θ0​. The parameter motion integrates the flow: θ˙=−η∑μ​∇θ​fμΔμ(t) with Δ(t)=e−ηtΘΔ(0) from (4.34), so

θ(t)−θ0​=−ημ∑​∇θ​fμ∫0t​ds(e−ηsΘ)μρ​Δρ(0)=−μ∑​∇θ​fμ[Θ−1(11−e−ηtΘ)]μρ​Δρ(0).

Contracting with ∇θ​f(x) and recognizing Θ(x,xμ)=∇θ​f(x)⋅∇θ​f(xμ) yields (4.36). (The test–train kernel is constant during training for the same reason the train–train one is: it is built from the frozen gradients at θ0​.)

From Exercise 4.3, we see that at the end of training t→∞ the network obeys

fθ∞​​(x)=fθ0​​(x)−Θ(x,xμ)Θμν−1​(fθ0​​(xν)−yν).

This is an affine-linear transformation of the Gaussian process fθ0​​(x) at initialization, so it is again a Gaussian process. It's straightforward to check that the new mean and covariance are

E[fθ∞​​(x)]Cov[fθ∞​​(x),fθ∞​​(x′)]​=ΘxμΘμν−1​yν=Kxx′−2ΘxμΘμν−1​Kνx′+ΘxμΘμν−1​KνρΘρσ−1​Θσx′,​

where Kxx′=K(x,x′), Θxμ=Θ(x,xμ), etc.

4.5 Summary

So far we've seen that with standard fan-in normalization (Section 3.2) at large width (N), and learning rate η scaled down by a factor N, we've got

∣Θ∣∼∣∇θ​f∣2∼N,∣ηΘ∣∼1,∣∇θ2​f∣∼1,∣θ−θ0​∣∼N​1​,∣fθ​−fθ0​​∣∼1,

which forces ηΘ to be constant and the network to linearize as a function of its parameters.

All this breaks down if

  • Depth L is large as well, with L/N nonzero. (See (Roberts et al. 2022, Ch. 11).)
  • Data samples n become large, with n/N nonzero.
  • Learning rate becomes large.

Both L and n large are interesting cases for modern neural networks!

Exercise 4.4 (The kernel freeze, empirically (lab)). Build a tiny regression task: n=8 random unit-norm inputs in d=4 with labels yμ∼N(0,1). For widths N∈{24,25,…,212}, initialize a one-hidden-layer tanh network with fan-in variances and train with full-batch gradient descent at learning rate η=η~​/N (fixed η~​) for a fixed number of steps, enough to drive the train loss below 10−3 at every width. Compute the empirical NTK Θμν (an n×n matrix of gradient inner products) at initialization and at the end of training. (a) Plot the relative kernel drift ∥Θend​−Θ0​∥F​/∥Θ0​∥F​ against N on log–log axes. (b) Plot the relative parameter displacement ∣θend​−θ0​∣/∣θ0​∣ likewise, and compare with the O(1/N​) bound (4.31). (c) For the widest network, compare the trained function on fresh test points with the frozen-kernel prediction (4.36).

Solution

Implementation notes: compute Θ from per-example gradients (an n×P Jacobian contracted with itself — with n=8 this is cheap at every width); use float64; train for a fixed horizon in the rescaled time η~​t so that widths are compared fairly. Expected results: (b) the parameter displacement decays with slope close to −1/2, matching (4.31). (a) The kernel drift decays with a slope between −1/2 and −1: the guaranteed bound from Section 4.3 is O(1/N​), while finite-width perturbation theory predicts (and one typically measures) the faster O(1/N); either way, the freeze is unmistakable on the plot. (c) At the largest width, the trained function on test points agrees with the frozen-kernel prediction (4.36) to within a few percent — and the agreement degrades as N shrinks, which is feature learning beginning to stir.

4.6 Bayesian learning at large width: kernel learning

So far, we have considered MLP's at large width, trained via gradient flow (as an approximation to SGD/GD). We found that their NTK remains constant and that their late-time distribution is a Gaussian process given by (4.38).

Suppose that we consider the same large-width network, but "train" Bayesian inference instead, on the empirical MSE loss L(θ)=nLn​(θ)=21​∑μ=1n​∣f(xμ)−yμ∣2. (Recall from Section 2.5 that, practically speaking, this means training via Langevin dynamics.) Then we expect a Bayesian posterior

P(θ)=Z1​e−βL(θ)π(θ),π(θ)∝e−σw​NL​​∣w(L+1)∣2−...−σw​d​∣w(1)∣2

where the prior π(θ) encodes the fan-in normalization of the weight variances.

We'd like to push the distribution forward to the network function fθ​(x). At large-width, the push-forward of the prior is our familiar Gaussian process from Section 3.4; expressed via a functional integral as in 3.5 it becomes

π[f]=Z′1​e−∫dxdx′f(x)K−1(x,x′)f(x′)

with K(x,x′)=Kˉ(L+1)(x,x′) the final-layer GP kernel. Since the loss is explicitly a function of network values, we immediately get the late-time trained distribution

P[f]=Z′′1​e−21​[β∑μ=1n​(f(xμ)−yμ)2+∫dxdx′f(x)K−1(x,x′)f(x′)]

Note that the action here is quadratic in function values, so this is still a Gaussian process!

Exercise 4.5 (Kernel ridge regression from the Gaussian posterior). Show that we can rewrite this distribution as a standard Gaussian

P[f]∝e−21​∫dxdx′[f(x)−μ(x)]Σ(x,x′)−1[f(x′)−μ(x′)]

with mean and covariance written in terms of the n×n matrix K^μν:=K(xμ,xν) (the untrained GP kernel evaluated on training data) as

μ(x)Σ(x,x′)​=μ,ν∑​K(x,xμ)(K^+β−1In​)μν−1​yν,=K(x,x′)−μ,ν∑​K(x,xμ)(K^+β−1In​)μν−1​K(xν,x′).​

(Hint: the exponent is quadratic in f; complete the square, using the Woodbury/Sherman–Morrison identity to relate the two natural forms of the answer.)

Solution

The exponent is quadratic in f, so the posterior is Gaussian and it suffices to find its mean and covariance. Varying the exponent with respect to f(x) gives the stationarity (mean) equation ∫dx′K−1(x,x′)μ(x′)+β∑μ​(μ(xμ)−yμ)δ(x−xμ)=0, i.e. μ(x)=−β∑μ​K(x,xμ)(μ(xμ)−yμ). Evaluating at the training points gives a closed linear system for the vector μ(xν), solved by μ(xν)=[K^(K^+β−1I)−1]νρ​yρ; substituting back yields the stated μ(x). The covariance is the inverse of the quadratic form, Σ=(K−1+βδdata​)−1, which the Woodbury identity converts into the stated form K−K(K^+β−1I)−1K (all data-indexed). The two limits are instructive: β→∞ gives noiseless GP interpolation, pinned exactly at the data; finite β is ridge regularization, with β−1 the ridge.

These equations embody what's sometimes known as kernel regression, with ridge parameter β−1=T. If the training samples are sufficiently dense, the mean can be an approximated by an integral in terms of the untrained kernel

μ(x)≈∫dx′dx′′K(x,x′)(K+(nβ)−1id)−1(x′,x′′)y(x′′).

Writing the data "truths" y(x)=∑yk​φk​(x) in an eigenbasis for K, with ordered eigenvalues λ1​≥λ2​≥..., we find

μ(x)=k=1∑∞​λk​+(nβ)−1λk​​yk​φk​(x)≈ks.t.λk​≳(nβ)−1∑​yk​φk​(x).

This is the Bayesian version of lazy learning. For given n,β, the "modes" of the data distribution with λk​≳(nβ)−1 are learned by the network, and the rest are projected out.

Recall that in the Bayesian context, the rescaled inverse-temperature nβ should play a role somewhat analogous to training time in SGD/GD. We can see this explicitly here. For example, in SGD/GD lazy learning, the characteristic time to learn an NTK mode sμ2​ is t≈1/sμ2​ (see (4.35)). Correspondingly, in Bayesian lazy learning, the minimum inverse-temperature required to learn a GP mode is βn≈1/λk​.

5. Mean-field scaling

Sections 3 and 4 analyzed one and the same large-width limit: fan-in initialization (Section 3.2), learning rate scaled down as η=η~​/N, width N→∞ at fixed depth and data. At initialization the network converges to a Gaussian process; during training the NTK freezes, the network linearizes, and (by the definition of Section 4.2) no features are learned. It is tempting to conclude that infinite width implies laziness. The lesson of this section is that it does not, and that laziness was a consequence of a choice of parametrization, rather than of width. Changing the normalization of the output layer by a single extra factor of N​ produces a different, equally well-defined infinite-width limit in which the network starts at zero, individual weights move an order-one distance, the NTK evolves in time, and features are genuinely learned.

This alternative limit is called the mean-field limit. The name comes by analogy to a classic setup in statistical physics: an interacting particle system with weak all-to-all couplings, whose N→∞ behavior is governed by a self-consistent "mean field." We'll first explain what physicists mean by a mean-field theory (Section 5.1), then run the analogy in detail for one-hidden-layer networks (Section 5.2), see how the NTK story of Section 4 changes (Section 5.3). Finally we'll discuss some practical applications, including interpolating scalings, μP, and what this framework is actually used for (Sections 5.4–5.5).

The mean-field limit of one-hidden-layer networks was constructed independently, and essentially simultaneously, by four groups (Mei et al. 2018; Chizat & Bach 2018; Rotskoff & Vanden-Eijnden 2022; Sirignano & Spiliopoulos 2020); our treatment draws on all of them. Pedagogical accounts may be found in (Spiliopoulos et al. 2025, Ch. 20) and (Hanin 2026, Lecture 4).

5.1 Mean-field theories in physics

"Mean-field theory" is one of the oldest and simplest approximation schemes in statistical mechanics: replace the fluctuating environment felt by each degree of freedom with its average (a macroscopic order parameter), then demand self-consistency upon recalculating this average. For most systems this is an uncontrolled approximation, though often a remarkably successful one cf. (Tong 2012, Chapter 1). There is, however, a family of models — those with weak, all-to-all couplings — for which it becomes exact as N→∞; and networks in mean-field scaling will turn out to be precisely such a model.

5.1.1 Warm-up: the Curie–Weiss magnet

The Curie–Weiss magnet is a simple microscopic model of magnetization, and a close cousin of the more famous Ising model.

The Ising model starts with an undirected graph Λ with N vertices. Typically Λ is a finite, regular lattice in D dimensions (for some choice of D). At each vertex i of Λ one places a binary degree of freedom si​∈{±1}, thought of as a magnetic spin. The energy of the system, for given choices of {si​}, depends on a "coupling strength" J and an "external magnetic field" B, and is given by

ENIsing​(s;J,B)=−Jedges⟨ij⟩∈Λ∑​si​sj​−Bi=1∑N​si​.

The partition function is

ZNIsing​(J,B,β)=s∈{±1}N∑​e−βENIsing​(s;J,B).

(As anticipated back in Section 2, the energy plays the role of a network's loss function.)

The Ising model is notoriously difficult to analyze exactly, even at large N. It depends strongly on the choice of dimension D. The Curie–Weiss model is a close cousin, which again has N spins si​, but rather than using including nearest-neighbor couplings along graph edges simply couples every spin to every other one, weakly, with coupling strength 1/N. (Equivalently, one chooses Λ to be the fully-connected graph.) The energy looks like

EN​(s)=−2N1​i,j=1∑N​si​sj​−Bi=1∑N​si​=−N(2m2​+Bm),m:=N1​i∑​si​.

As shown, it can be rewriten entirely in terms of the average spin m, known as the magnetization. m will serve as the order parameter of this system, in the sense of Section 2. The coupling strength 1/N is required to ensure that the total force felt by any one spin from the N others remains of order one, and that the total energy EN​ remains extensive.

Explicitly, the field (or force) felt by a single spin si​ is

−∂si​∂EN​​=N1​j∑​sj​+B=m+B.

Spin i does not care about any individual other spin; it feels only the empirical average m. That average is the "mean field." The classic argument then has three features:

  1. Each degree of freedom couples to the others only through an average. (True by construction here.)
  2. The average barely fluctuates. If the spins are roughly independent, the CLT makes the fluctuations of m of size O(1/N​); as N→∞ each spin sees a deterministic effective field m+B.
  3. The average is fixed self-consistently. A single independent spin in field m+B, at inverse-temperature β (Section 2.2), has partition function Zi​=∑si​=±1​eβ(m+B)si​=2cosh(β(m+B)), and expectation value
E(si​)=Zi​1​si​=±1∑​si​eβ(m+B)si​=tanh(β(m+B)).

But m was defined as the average spin, so consistency requires

m=tanh(β(m+B)).

Equation (5.6) is the prototype of every mean-field theory: solve the one-particle problem in the average environment, then demand that the average you get out equals the average you put in. For a finite-dimensional lattice magnet, where each spin has a few strongly-coupled neighbors, steps 1–2 are approximations (a spin's neighbors fluctuate along with it). For the 1/N all-to-all model they become exact as N→∞: the mean field is an average of N weakly-correlated terms, and the law of large numbers kills its fluctuations.

Exercise 5.1 (Curie–Weiss and its phase transition). (a) At B=0, show that m=0 is the only solution of (5.6) for β<1, while two symmetric solutions ±m∗(β) appear for β>1, with m∗∝(β−1)1/2 near the transition. Try to argue that this is a second-order phase transition, in the taxonomy of Section 2.4. (b) Hold β>1 fixed and vary B from positive to negative. Show that a first-order phase transition occurs at Bc​=0, as two local minima of the free energy exchange dominance and the magnetization jumps from +m∗ to −m∗. (c) Solve (5.6) numerically by fixed-point iteration m(k+1)=tanh(β(m(k)+B)) and watch the iteration converge. Keep this iteration in mind: we will meet its infinite-dimensional cousin below.

Solution

(a) At B=0 the line m and the curve tanh(βm) intersect only at m=0 when the slope β≤1; for β>1 two symmetric solutions ±m∗ appear. Expanding tanh to cubic order, m=βm−31​(βm)3, gives m∗≈3(β−1)​ near the transition: the order parameter is continuous with a square-root singularity — a second-order transition in the taxonomy of Section 2.4 (no competing basins; one basin deforms). (b) Trading the sum over spins for an integral over m (with the binary entropy H(21+m​) of Equation 2.41 counting configurations) gives Z≈∫dme−NS(m) with action S(m;B)=−H(21+m​)−β(2m2​+Bm). For β>1 and ∣B∣ small, S has two local minima m±​≈±m∗, and the B-term tilts the balance: S(m+​;B)−S(m−​;B)≈−2βBm∗, so the branch values cross at Bc​=0 with distinct slopes ∂B​S(m±​)=−β(±m∗). This is the two-branch mechanism of Section 2.4 verbatim, with B as the control parameter: the global minimizer, and with it the magnetization m=−β1​∂B​Smin​, jumps from +m∗ to −m∗ as B crosses zero — a first-order transition. (At finite N the jump is a logistic sigmoid of width ∼1/(Nβm∗); and past the crossing each minimum survives as a metastable state out to a spinodal field ±Bsp​(β), the origin of hysteresis in real magnets.) (c) The iteration converges geometrically to the stable fixed point (the nonzero one when β>1, if seeded away from the unstable m=0); its infinite-dimensional cousin is the fixed-point iteration for the McKean–Vlasov equation in Section 5.2.

5.1.2 The general shape of a mean-field model

Nothing in the story above needed binary spins. More abstractly, one can take N "particles" θi​∈Rp with an extensive energy of the form

EN​(θ)=i=1∑N​V(θi​)+2N1​i,j=1∑N​U(θi​,θj​),

with a single-particle potential V and a symmetric pair interaction U, again with the characteristic 1/N coupling. The force felt by particle θi​ is −∇θi​​EN​. More so, for particles dominated by drag (highly viscous motion), the dynamics at zero temperature are governed by familiar gradient-descent equations

θ˙i​=−∇θi​​EN​=−∇V(θi​)−N1​j=1∑N​∇1​U(θi​,θj​),

where ∇1​ differentiates the first slot of U. Once more each particle feels only an empirical average of forces.

It is worth packaging this observation in a way that will carry over verbatim to networks. Define the empirical measure

ρN​:=N1​i=1∑N​δ(θ−θi​),

a probability measure on Rp recording where the collection of N particles sit. Then (5.8) says that every particle descends one and the same effective single-particle potential, shaped by where everyone currently is:

θ˙i​=−∇θ​Ψ(θi​;ρN​),Ψ(θ;ρ):=V(θ)+∫U(θ,θ′)dρ(θ′).

The particles are coupled only through ρN​ — the exact analogue of "every spin feels only m." The same three-step argument as before then suggests that as N→∞ the empirical measure becomes deterministic and self-consistent. We will carry this out carefully, for networks, in the next subsection.

5.2 Mean-field scaling for one-hidden-layer networks

Return to the one-hidden-layer network of Sections 3.5 and 4.3, but now normalized with 1/N out front and order-one weights:

fθ​(x)=N1​i=1∑N​ci​ϕ(ai​⋅x),ci​∼N(0,1),ai​∼N(0,d1​Id​),

with ci​∈R, ai​,x∈Rd. Compare with Sections 3–4: there, fan-in initialization gave f=∑i​c~i​ϕ(ai​⋅x) with c~i​∼N(0,σw​/N), i.e. c~i​=O(1/N​), which is the same as an explicit prefactor 1/N​ with order-one weights. Mean-field scaling suppresses the output by one extra factor of 1/N​. The function class is identical — only the coordinates on it have changed. However, gradient flow is not invariant under reparametrization: as emphasized in Section 4.1.1, gradient descent presupposes the Euclidean metric on parameter space, and rescaling coordinates rescales that metric. Two parametrizations of the same function class can (and here will) flow along completely different trajectories.

For a mean-field analysis, our N particles are going to be the N hidden neurons, with parameters

θi​=(ci​,ai​)∈Rd+1,i=1,...,N.

Their values are encoded in the empirical measure (5.9), and the network (5.11) depends on its parameters only through ρN​,

fθ​(x)=∫cϕ(a⋅x)dρN​(c,a)=:fρN​​(x).

We think of the network value fρ​ as a linear functional of ρ. Neurons are viewed as exchangeable particles, and the measure is their state.

5.2.1 Initialization

At initialization, the summands ci​ϕ(ai​⋅x) in (5.11) are i.i.d. with mean zero (since ci​ is independent of ai​ and E[ci​]=0). With the 1/N prefactor, the law of large numbers gives, for each fixed x,

fθ0​​(x)==0E[cϕ(a⋅x)]​​+O(1/N​)N→∞​0.

Contrast this with Section 3.4: with the 1/N​ normalization, the same sum sits exactly at the scale of its fluctuations, and the CLT produces an order-one Gaussian process. Mean-field scaling instead sits at the scale of the mean.

The network begins training as (essentially) the zero function; there is no random-function prior to speak of, and whatever the trained network becomes is built by training rather than inherited from initialization.

5.2.2 The loss is a mean-field energy

Let's train on MSE loss over the data (xμ,yμ)μ=1n​, as in Section 4:

L(θ)=21​μ=1∑n​(fθ​(xμ)−yμ)2.

Inserting (5.11) and expanding the square, we get

L(θ)=const+N1​i=1∑N​V(θi​)+2N21​i,j=1∑N​U(θi​,θj​),

with

V(θ)=−μ=1∑n​yμcϕ(a⋅xμ),U(θ,θ′)=μ=1∑n​cϕ(a⋅xμ)c′ϕ(a′⋅xμ).

Comparing (5.16) with (5.7), we see that up to an overall factor of N, the loss is precisely a mean-field energy. In particular, EN​:=NL has the canonical normalization from (5.7) and is extensive, while the loss itself can be interpreted as the intensive energy per neuron.

We can also identify physical roles for the two potentials! V rewards neurons for aligning their output function cϕ(a⋅⋅) with the data, playing the role of the external field B; while U is a data-weighted interaction between pairs of neurons that penalizes redundant features, playing the role of the spin-spin coupling.

5.2.3 Equations of motion and the mean field

Because ∂f/∂θi​=O(1/N) in this parametrization, raw gradients of L are O(1/N), and gradient flow at fixed learning rate would freeze as N→∞. We must therefore scale the learning rate up,

η=Nη~​,

with η~​ fixed. (Equivalently, we could run vanilla gradient flow on the extensive energy EN​=NL.) Note the contrast with Section 4.3: there the NTK grew like N and we scaled the learning rate down by N; here (as we'll verify in Section 5.3) the NTK shrinks like 1/N and we scale up.

With (5.18), the flow θ˙=−η∇θ​L becomes, per neuron,

c˙i​=−η~​μ=1∑n​Δμϕ(ai​⋅xμ),a˙i​=−η~​ci​μ=1∑n​Δμϕ′(ai​⋅xμ)xμ,

where Δμ=fρN​​(xμ)−yμ is the residual of Section 4.1. Equivalently, in the potential form (5.10),

θ˙i​=−η~​∇θ​Ψ(θi​;ρN​),Ψ(θ;ρ)=V(θ)+∫U(θ,θ′)dρ(θ′)=μ=1∑n​Δρμ​cϕ(a⋅xμ),

with Δρμ​=fρ​(xμ)−yμ.

As anticipated, the velocity of neuron i depends on its own state (ci​,ai​), and on all the other neurons only through the average fρN​​=N1​∑j​cj​ϕ(aj​⋅⋅), via the residual Δμ. The network function f is the mean field here! We arrive at a dictionary:

Curie–Weissspin si​∈{±1}magnetization m=N1​∑j​sj​external field hpair coupling −N1​si​sj​effective field m+Bextensive energy EN​zero-temperature dynamicsLangevin at temperature Tm=tanh(β(m+B))​one-hidden-layer network, mean-field scalingneuron θi​=(ci​,ai​)∈Rd+1network function fρ​=N1​∑j​cj​ϕ(aj​⋅⋅)data term V (the targets yμ)neuron-neuron interaction N1​U(θi​,θj​)residual Δρμ​=fρ​(xμ)−yμNL(the loss is intensive)gradient flownoisy training, Section 2.5self-consistent Gibbs measure, Equation 5.27 below​​

Exercise 5.2 (Structure of the mean-field equations). (a) Derive (5.16)–(5.17) and (5.19), and check that (5.20) reproduces them, using the symmetry of U. (b) (Balancedness.) For a positively homogeneous activation such as ReLU, ϕ′(z)z=ϕ(z). Show that in this case (5.19) conserves ci2​−∣ai​∣2 for every neuron, exactly, along the flow. The two layers of a given neuron therefore remain coupled for all time. (On the other hand, distinct neurons will decouple from each other, as we'll see momentarily.) (c) Observe that for MSE loss c˙i​ in (5.19) does not depend on ci​ (only on ai​ and the mean field). Where does the linearity of fρ​ in c enter?

Solution

(a) Expanding the square in the loss and collecting single-sum and double-sum terms gives (5.16)–(5.17) directly. For the equations of motion, ∂fρN​​(xμ)/∂ci​=N1​ϕ(ai​⋅xμ) and ∂fρN​​(xμ)/∂ai​=N1​ci​ϕ′(ai​⋅xμ)xμ; the chain rule plus η=Nη~​ gives (5.19). Writing the same gradient through Ψ, the symmetry U(θ,θ′)=U(θ′,θ) ensures the double sum contributes twice the one-sided derivative, matching (5.20). (b) From (5.19): ci​c˙i​=−η~​ci​∑μ​Δμϕ(ai​⋅xμ) and ai​⋅a˙i​=−η~​ci​∑μ​Δμϕ′(ai​⋅xμ)(ai​⋅xμ). For positively homogeneous ϕ, ϕ′(z)z=ϕ(z), so the two right-hand sides coincide and dtd​(ci2​−∣ai​∣2)=2(ci​c˙i​−ai​⋅a˙i​)=0. (c) Because fρ​ is linear in the output weights, ∂f/∂ci​ contains no ci​; the only route by which ci​ influences c˙i​ is through the mean field Δμ — i.e. through the population average, weighted by 1/N. This linearity is also what makes the loss a quadratic (rather than higher-order) polynomial in each particle, i.e. what limits the interaction to be pairwise.

5.2.4 From particles to measures: the continuity equation

We now pass to the N→∞ limit, in distinct steps.

Step 1: rewrite the N coupled ODEs as one equation for the empirical measure. (This remains exact at finite N.) Suppose particles move deterministically with some velocity field, θ˙t​=vt​(θt​), and let ρt​ denote the law of one such particle.

The expectation of a smooth test function g obeys

dtd​∫gdρt​=dtd​E[g(θt​)]=E[∇g(θt​)⋅vt​(θt​)]=∫∇g⋅vt​dρt​=−∫g∇⋅(ρt​vt​),

integrating by parts in the last step. Since g was arbitrary,

∂t​ρt​+∇⋅(ρt​vt​)=0.

This is known as the continuity equation, and it simply expresses conservation of probability. Applied to our system, with vt​=−η~​∇Ψ(⋅;ρN,t​) from (5.20), the empirical measure satisfies (weakly, since it is a sum of delta functions)

∂t​ρN,t​=η~​∇⋅(ρN,t​∇θ​Ψ(θ;ρN,t​)).

An important consequence of the mean-field (1/N, all-to-all) coupling here is that (5.24) is a closed equation in ρN​.

Step 2: the limit. At finite N, ρN,t​ is a random, atomic measure. (Atomic means it's a sum of delta functions; it's random due to random initialization.) As N→∞ with i.i.d. initialization θi​∼ρ0​, the law of large numbers suggests — and the theorems of (Mei et al. 2018; Chizat & Bach 2018; Rotskoff & Vanden-Eijnden 2022; Sirignano & Spiliopoulos 2020) confirm — that ρN,t​ converges (weakly) to ρt​, a deterministic curve of smooth probability measures solving the limiting PDE

∂t​ρt​=η~​∇⋅(ρt​∇θ​(V+U∗ρt​)),with(U∗ρ)(θ):=∫U(θ,θ′)dρ(θ′).

There are quantitative O(1/N​) error bounds at any fixed time horizon.

5.2.5 The McKean–Vlasov equation and self-consistency

In this context, the analogue of the Curie–Weiss self-consistency (5.6), namely m=tanh(β(m+B)), is called the McKean–Vlasov equation. To get it, focus on a single representative neuron θi​. As N→∞, we can replace the force on it by the ensemble average:

θˉ˙t​=−η~​∇θ​Ψ(θˉt​;ρt​),subject toρt​=Law(θˉt​).

The constraint ρt​=Law(θˉt​) is the entire content of the equation: the particle is driven by a field built from a distribution, and that distribution is its own law.

(Probabilists call (5.26) a nonlinear Markov process, nonlinear not in θ but in the law.) The McKeen–Vlasov equation is equivalent to the continuity equation; the particle trajectories of (5.26) are the characteristic curves of the PDE (5.25).

We remark on a few structural features:

  • Propagation of chaos. Since neurons interact only through a quantity (ρN​, equivalently fρN​​) that becomes deterministic as N→∞, they become asymptotically independent: any fixed collection of k neurons converges to k i.i.d. copies of (5.26), with cross-neuron correlations of size O(1/N). Thus, independence at initialization propagates instead of degrading (Sznitman 1991).
  • Gradient-flow structure. Define the N→∞ loss as a functional of the measure, L[ρ]=21​∑μ​(fρ​(xμ)−yμ)2. Since fρ​ is linear in ρ, this functional is convex in ρ.

This ultimately leads to global-convergence theorems. For example, it was shown in (Chizat & Bach 2018) that for homogeneous activations (e.g. ReLU), if training converges at all, it converges to a global minimizer of the convex functional L[ρ].

  • Temperature. If one trains instead with the Langevin dynamics of Section 2.5, Eqn. (2.48), at temperature T=β−1, one finds convergence to a stationary distribution that satisfies (Mei et al. 2018)
ρ∞​(θ)∝e−βΨ(θ;ρ∞​).

This is another version of the "m=tanh(β(m+B))" consistency condition, now for noisy training.

How would one actually solve the self-consistent system (5.26)? The same way one solves (5.6) (Exercise 5.1(c)): freeze a guessed environment (ρt​), solve the now-ordinary ODE, compute the law of the solution, feed it back, iterate. On short time horizons this map is a contraction, which is how existence, uniqueness, and propagation of chaos are all proven in one stroke (Sznitman 1991). Alternatively, solve the PDE (5.25) on a grid, which is feasible (only) for small d.

In Figure 5 we instead solve the system by simply training a network with d=1. In the left panel, each dot is a neuron. Training is a flow of the cloud of neurons, and the the cloud condenses onto the low-dimensional structures in weight space that realize the target — learning its features.

5.3 The NTK is no longer constant: feature learning

Section 4.3 showed that in fan-in scaling the (normalized) NTK freezes as N→∞, and Section 4.2 defined feature learning as change of the NTK during training. Let's redo that computation in mean-field scaling. From (5.11), ∂f/∂ci​=N1​ϕ(ai​⋅x) and ∂f/∂ai​=N1​ci​ϕ′(ai​⋅x)x, so the NTK of Section 4.1 is

Θ(x,x′)=N21​i=1∑N​kθi​​(x,x′)=N1​∫kθ​(x,x′)dρN​(θ),

with the per-neuron kernel

kθ​(x,x′):=ϕ(a⋅x)ϕ(a⋅x′)+c2ϕ′(a⋅x)ϕ′(a⋅x′)x⋅x′.

Thus Θ=O(1/N), recovering the previous observation that gradients are small, which was the reason for the rescaling (5.18). As N→∞, meaningful object is NΘ=∫kθ​dρN​, and the function-space dynamics (4.10) now becomes a kernel gradient flow with a time-dependent kernel:

dtd​fμ=−η~​(NΘμν​)​ρt​​Δν,NΘ​ρt​​=∫kθ​dρt​.

At initialization the LLN makes NΘ→Eρ0​​[kθ​], a deterministic kernel — the same limiting kernel as in fan-in scaling, with matched variances. The two limits start from the same place.

During training, however, they part ways. In Section 4.3, each parameter moved only O(1/N​), so ρN​ stayed within O(1/N​) of ρ0​ and the kernel was pinned: ∥Θ(t)/N−Θ(0)/N∥=O(1/N) there. Here, the equations of motion (5.19) move each particle an order-one distance. (Each neuron has only O(1/N) leverage, so fitting the data forces the average neuron to move a distance O(1).) Thus ρt​ transports macroscopically, and by (5.30) the kernel is dragged along at order one as well.

5.4 The scaling dial and Maximal Update Parameterization

It's quite instructive to look at an entire one-parameter family of scalings, which has fan-in/NTK scaling and mean-field scaling as its endpoints. The family can be encoded via a prefactor

fθ​(x)=Nγ1​i=1∑N​ci​ϕ(ai​⋅x),γ∈[21​,1],

where ci​∼N(0,I). For each γ, as N→∞, the learning rate must be simultaneously be scaled as η=N2γ−1η~​ so that the function-space dynamics stays O(1) (one can derive that from Θ∼N1−2γ). Repeating the estimates above gives (see Exercise 5.3):

γ=21​21​<γ<1γ=1​fθ0​​ at initO(1) (GP, CLT)O(N21​−γ)→0O(N−1/2)→0​per-neuron motionO(N−1/2)O(Nγ−1)→0O(1)​limitlazy: Sections Section 3–Section 4lazy (frozen kernel, zero init)mean-field: this section​​

Notably, every intermediate γ collapses onto the kernel limit: the initialization GP is scaled away, but the neurons still move vanishingly little, so training is again linear in an (appropriately rescaled) frozen kernel (Chizat et al. 2019; Mei et al. 2018). Mean-field, γ=1, is the unique scaling in this family with both a well-defined limit and order-one feature movement; it's the "maximal update" that one can take without blowing up. This uniqueness can be generalized from one hidden layer to arbitrary depth (where consistency forces layer-dependent learning-rate and initialization scalings), and is known as the Maximal Update Parametrization, μP, in Yang and Hu's line of work on tensor programs (Yang & Hu 2021). In particular, mean-field scaling is μP for L=1.

Exercise 5.3 (Lazy vs. rich along the dial). For the family (5.31): (a) show Θ=O(N1−2γ) and hence that η=N2γ−1η~​ is the right co-scaling; (b) show the initialization output is O(N1/2−γ) and per-neuron velocities are O(Nγ−1); (c) conclude that the (normalized) kernel drift over any fixed training horizon is O(Nγ−1), vanishing for every γ<1; (d) reconcile γ=21​ with the bounds of Section 4.3. Optional: relate γ to the output-scale parameter α of (Chizat et al. 2019), where multiplying any model by α→∞ produces lazy training.

Solution

(a) ∂f/∂ci​=N−γϕ(ai​⋅x) and similarly for ai​, so Θ=∑i​N−2γkθi​​=N1−2γ⋅N1​∑i​kθi​​=O(N1−2γ); demanding ηΘ=O(1) forces η=N2γ−1η~​. (b) At initialization f=N−γ∑i​ci​ϕ(ai​⋅x) is N−γ times a sum of N i.i.d. mean-zero terms =O(N​), so fθ0​​=O(N1/2−γ). Per-neuron velocities: c˙i​=−η∂L/∂ci​=O(N2γ−1⋅N−γ)=O(Nγ−1), and likewise for a˙i​. (c) The normalized kernel N2γ−1Θ=N1​∑i​kθi​​ is an empirical average over particles, so over any fixed horizon its drift is of the order of the per-particle displacement, O(Nγ−1) — vanishing for every γ<1, order one exactly at γ=1. (d) At γ=21​: per-neuron motion O(N−1/2), matching the bound (4.31); initialization output O(1), the GP of Section 3. For the optional part: relative to the mean-field parametrization (5.11), fγ​=αfMF​ with α=N1−γ, so in the language of (Chizat et al. 2019) every γ<1 sends the laziness α→∞ with width — lazy — while γ=1 keeps α of order one.

5.5 What is this framework good for?

Nobody solves the McKean–Vlasov PDE (5.25) for a real network! There are practical payoffs, though, of three different kinds: scaling prescriptions, mechanism identification, and reduced descriptions that downstream theories build on.

Hyperparameter transfer (μP) is one key application. The mean-field analysis is, fundamentally, a theory of which joint scalings of initialization and learning rate keep the training dynamics nondegenerate and learning features as N→∞. Its deep-network generalization (Yang & Hu 2021) turns this into an engineering recipe, μTransfer (Yang et al. 2022): parametrize the network so that its infinite-width limit is the feature-learning one, and then optimal hyperparameters become approximately width-independent, so one can tune a small proxy model and transfer the settings to the large one. In the original demonstration this retuned GPT-3 6.7B at a few percent of pretraining cost and outperformed the published model; variants of this parametrization are now standard in large-scale training.

The dial of Section 5.4 also lets one interpolate between regimes on real architectures, and measure where feature learning actually pays off. Kernel-regime behavior tends to be competitive on small datasets, while on CIFAR-scale image tasks trained networks beat their own frozen NTKs by large margins (Geiger et al. 2020). Diagnostics from this circle of ideas (kernel distance/alignment during training, e.g. the silent-alignment effect (Atanasov et al. 2022)) are now routine tools for asking "is my network actually learning features, or just doing kernel regression?"

The mean-field limit here holds data fixed while sending N→∞, which unfortunately does not yet make it a quantitative theory of generalization at realistic data/width ratios. The dynamical mean-field theory of Section 6 (Bordelon & Pehlevan 2022) will rectify this somewhat; it is a field-theoretic refinement of the current analysis, whose extensions do reproduce compute-optimal neural scaling laws, in particular at large dataset size (Bordelon et al. 2024).

5.6 Grokking as a lazy-to-rich transition: a reading exercise

We finish this section with two guided readings that apply various concepts introduced above to one of the most interesting and fundamental phenomenons in learning: grokking (Power et al. 2022). Grokking refers to the following behavior. One trains a small network on an algorithmic dataset — the canonical example is addition mod P, presented as pairs (n,m) with label (n+m)modP, with only a fraction of all P2 facts shown. The network reaches perfect training accuracy quickly, while test accuracy sits at chance: it has simply memorized. Then, orders of magnitude later in training and long after the train loss has flattened, test accuracy jumps abruptly to near 100%. Such delayed, abrupt generalization, with emergent capabilities, demands a mechanism.

Theory has produced (at least) two quantitative explanations, and this subsection and the next walk through one each: the dynamical lens of Kumar–Bordelon–Gershman–Pehlevan (Kumar et al. 2024) (this subsection) — grokking as a delayed transition from lazy to rich dynamics — and the equilibrium lens of Rubin–Seroussi–Ringel (Rubin et al. 2024) (Section 5.7) — grokking as a first-order phase transition with metastable lag. The two walkthroughs are parallel in structure and use largely disjoint toolkits from these notes. The dynamical one presumes comfort with Sections 4 and 5.4; the Bayesian one is a denser read, and combines scaling analysis with a mean-field approximation.

The work of Kumar, Bordelon, Gershman, and Pehlevan (Kumar et al. 2024) invokes no statistical-mechanics ensemble at all. There is only gradient descent, and the lazy/rich dial of Section 5.4, unfolding in time. The paper claims that a network groks when 1) it first fits the training data through its cheap, fast channel (kernel regression with the frozen NTK of its initialization), and that lazy fit memorizes without generalizing because the initial kernel is misaligned with the task; then 2) on a slower timescale controlled by the network's laziness, the features finally move (the kernel rotates, as in Section 5.3), a generalizing solution is found, and test loss falls long after train loss did. Two beautiful features of this work are that its clearest examples grok under vanilla gradient descent with zero weight decay, and that the parameter norm increases during grokking. Both are direct counterexamples to earlier accounts of grokking built on weight decay and shrinking norms.

The paper is written almost entirely in the language these notes have already built (Sections 4 and 5), so the dialect box below is short. Read the introduction, the two-layer polynomial-regression model, and the experiments (modular arithmetic, MNIST, a one-layer transformer); skip the dynamical mean-field asymptotics on a first pass — that machinery belongs to Section 6. Then work through Exercise 5.4.

A few translation of terminology from (Kumar et al. 2024):

  • Lazy / linearized dynamics: the regime of Section 4.3 — the network moves only in the affine subspace (4.1) spanned by its initial gradients, so training is kernel regression with the frozen initial NTK (Sections 4.1, 4.6).
  • Laziness parameter α: an overall multiplier on the network output, f↦αf (with loss and learning rate co-scaled). This is the continuous version of the γ-dial of Section 5.4, in the form introduced by (Chizat et al. 2019): α→∞ is fully lazy, small α is rich.
  • Kernel–task (mis)alignment: the language of Section 4.2 — how much of the target lies in the top eigenmodes of the initial NTK. Misaligned = the target's weight sits in small-eigenvalue modes, which the mode-filtering formula of Section 4.6 says are not learnable from the available data.
  • Sufficient statistics: a handful of scalar functions of the weights whose closed dynamics determine the test loss — the dynamical analogue of the order parameters of Section 2.

Exercise 5.4 (★) (Grokking as a lazy-to-rich transition). Read (Kumar et al. 2024) as assigned above, and answer the following, citing where in the paper each answer lives. (Parts (a)–(e) have exact counterparts in Exercise 5.5, the other walkthrough; part (f) is the shared comparison question.)

(a) What regime is the analysis set in, and what dial controls it? There is no thermodynamic limit and no equilibrium ensemble here, so what plays the role that a "scaling limit" plays elsewhere in this section? How is the laziness parameter α implemented, and how does it relate to the γ-dial of Section 5.4? Section 5.2's scaling prescription had two halves, an output scale and a learning-rate scale. Which half is doing the work here? (The other walkthrough meets the opposite half: see Exercise 5.5(a).)

(b) What plays the role of the order parameter? What quantity distinguishes the memorized state from the generalizing one, and how would you measure it in a real training run? Compare with the Fourier overlap Φ(w) that plays this role in the other walkthrough (Exercise 5.5(b)): what information do the two quantities share?

(c) Necessary conditions. The paper states three conditions for grokking to occur. Find them, and translate each into the language of these notes (Sections 4.6, 4.3, 5.4).

(d) What parameter is tuned? What makes grokking more dramatic, and what makes it vanish entirely? What does the theory predict in the two extremes α→∞ and α small? Contrast with the control parameters of Exercise 5.5(d).

(e) Where does the delay come from? Both theories must explain the gap between the train-loss drop and the test-loss jump. Here there is no metastability and no noise — so what produces two well-separated timescales in a single deterministic flow? What does each theory require to produce a delay (noise? weight decay? neither?), and how do the paper's zero-weight-decay, growing-norm experiments bear on earlier explanations of grokking?

(f) Synthesis. Are the equilibrium mechanism of Section 5.7 and the dynamical mechanism of this section incompatible, or two corners of one phenomenon? Design at least one experiment whose outcome would favor one over the other — consider, e.g., how the grokking delay should depend on training noise at fixed hyperparameters, or how the delay should fluctuate from seed to seed, under each mechanism.

Solution

(a) Finite network, deterministic gradient descent/flow, no limit required: the analysis is organized around the linearization of Section 4.3 and departures from it. The dial is an output multiplier α (with appropriate co-scaling of the loss/learning rate), exactly the scale parameter of lazy training (Chizat et al. 2019): at large α an O(1) change of f requires only an O(1/α) change of weights, so features barely move — a continuous, finite-N version of the γ-dial, where Nγ−1 played the role of 1/α (Exercise 5.3). And this paper is precisely about the half of the scaling story that the Bayesian treatment of Exercise 5.5(a) could not see: there, only the induced function prior survived and the learning-rate/dynamics half dropped out; here there is no prior at all, and everything is the dynamics half — the two walkthroughs literally partition Section 5.2's prescription between them.

(b) The alignment between the (current) NTK and the task — equivalently the kernel's distance from its initialization, or the paper's low-dimensional sufficient statistics: in the memorized state the kernel is still (close to) its initialization and the fit lives in misaligned modes; in the generalizing state the kernel's top eigenspaces have rotated onto the target. Measurable in any run by tracking the empirical NTK (Section 4.2). The Fourier overlap Φ(w) of Exercise 5.5(b) carries the same information — features aligned with the task's structure — read off the weights and their posterior rather than off the kernel; for modular addition, a rotated kernel and condensed Fourier modes are two descriptions of the same event.

(c) (i) The top eigenvectors of the initial NTK are misaligned with the labels: in the language of Section 4.6, the target's weight sits in modes with small eigenvalues, so the lazy (kernel-regression) solution fits the training points without generalizing — memorization, in the precise mode-filtering sense. (ii) The dataset is in a Goldilocks window: large enough that a generalizing solution exists (cf. the critical sample size of Exercise 5.5(d)), small enough that train and test loss do not simply track each other. (iii) Training starts lazy (large α, or large initialization scale): feature learning is initially suppressed, as in Section 4.3, so the kernel fit happens first.

(d) The laziness α (and the initialization scale, which acts similarly): increasing it stretches the delay between the lazy fit and feature learning, making grokking more dramatic; decreasing it makes the network rich from the start, so train and test fall together and grokking vanishes. In the extreme α→∞ the network is a pure kernel machine forever: by condition (i) it never generalizes, and the grokking time diverges. Contrast Exercise 5.5(d): there the knobs were sample size and temperature moving the system across a phase boundary; here the knob does not change where the system ends up so much as how long the misaligned detour lasts.

(e) From a separation of timescales built into the flow: fitting the train set within the frozen-kernel subspace is fast (the exponential convergence of Section 4, eq. (4.34)), while rotating the kernel is slow — suppressed by the laziness, since feature motion is O(1/α)-small per unit of function change. Train loss bottoms out on the fast clock; test loss must wait for the slow one. Nothing stochastic is needed: no noise, no weight decay, no barrier crossing — and that is the force of the paper's counterexamples, since grokking with zero weight decay and growing weight norm rules out explanations in which regularization-driven norm shrinkage causes the transition. The equilibrium mechanism of Section 5.7, by contrast, needs temperature: its delay is the escape from a metastable free-energy basin, which pure gradient flow would never make.

(f) They live in different corners and need not compete: Rubin et al. describe noisy (Langevin/Bayesian) training near equilibrium, Kumar et al. deterministic training far from it; both say the cheap channel is used first — kernel fit or metastable memorizing phase — and features arrive late. Distinguishing experiments: (a) noise dependence — an activated (metastable-escape) delay should shorten rapidly with increasing training noise, roughly Arrhenius-like, while a timescale-separation delay survives at zero noise and depends on it only weakly; measure grokking time vs. Langevin temperature at fixed α, n. (b) Seed-to-seed statistics — nucleation out of a metastable state is a rare-event process with broad (roughly exponential) waiting-time distributions across seeds; a deterministic mechanism predicts narrow, initialization-scale-set delays. (c) The α-dial itself — the lazy-to-rich account makes a sharp prediction that the delay is monotonically stretched by α with grokking eliminated at small α; the equilibrium account ties the delay to the free-energy landscape at fixed ensemble, not to α. Running these on modular addition is a very feasible project.

5.7 Bayesian grokking: a first-order transition (alternative reading)

The alternative walkthrough takes the opposite starting point. Delayed, abrupt generalization should by now also trigger a reflex from Section 2.4: competing branches of a free energy, a first-order transition, and a metastable lag, exactly as dissected for the Ising perceptron in Section 2.4.1. The paper (Rubin et al. 2024) makes this reflex precise, and it is a fitting capstone for these notes: it assembles, in one real (if small) deep-learning phenomenon, nearly every tool we have developed: the Gibbs posterior of noisy training (Section 2.5), GP kernels and kernel regression (Sections 3.3, 4.6), mean-field scaling and self-consistency (this section), and the anatomy of first-order transitions (Section 2.4). It is, however, a genuinely dense paper, written in an idiosyncratic dialect of the "adaptive kernel" school (Seroussi et al. 2023). This subsection is therefore structured as a reading exercise in the style of Section 1: the goal is to recognize the structures, not to verify the computations. Read the paper's introduction, setup, and modular-arithmetic results (do not read the appendices on a first pass), then work through Exercise 5.5.

Warm-up. Before any statistical mechanics, it helps to know concretely what the network is trying to become. Gromov (Gromov 2023) writes down exact weights for a two-layer network with quadratic activation that solve modular addition: the first-layer weights are plane waves on ZP​ — entries cos(2πkn/P), sin(2πkn/P) at various frequencies k — and the quadratic activation's product-to-sum identities convert them into the required functions of (n+m)modP. Skim (Gromov 2023) just long enough to believe this. The lesson is that "the Fourier coefficients of the first-layer weights" becomes the obvious coordinate system for measuring how much structure a network has actually learned.

Some translations from the paper's language into that of these notes:

  • Langevin training at equilibrium: as in Section 2.5 verbatim: noisy gradient descent with weight decay; at late times, the Gibbs posterior; the weight decay γ sets the Gaussian prior and the noise level sets the temperature.
  • (Adaptive) kernel: the GP kernels of Section 3.3, but evaluated in the posterior rather than the prior, self-consistently: the kernel determines the posterior over hidden weights, which determines the kernel. This is a finite-temperature sibling of the self-consistent Gibbs measure (5.27).
  • Equivalent kernel (EK) approximation: the dense-data approximation of Section 4.6, where sums over training points are replaced by integrals over the input distribution. This is a cousin of an annealed approximation.
  • Mean-field scaling: the readout starts with variance σa2​/N, and σa2​→0 as N→∞; how this relates to the 1/N of (5.11) is Exercise 5.5(a).
  • GFL ("Gaussian feature learning") phase: refers to a disordered phase, in which the single-neuron posterior is a Gaussian, centered at zero overlap with the teacher's structure; the kernel adapts only perturbatively.
  • Mixed phase: a finite fraction of neurons shift to nonzero overlap (here: onto Fourier modes of the task) while the rest remain Gaussian; this coexistence is a signal of a first-order transition, cf. Section 2.4.1.

Exercise 5.5 (★) (Grokking as a first-order phase transition). Read (Rubin et al. 2024) as assigned above, and answer the following, citing where in the paper each answer lives. (Parts (a)–(e) have exact counterparts in Exercise 5.4, the other walkthrough; its part (f) is the shared comparison question.)

(a) What scaling limit is taken? Look for where the output-layer weight decay is fixed, and for the phrase "mean-field scaling." How does the paper's scaling relate to the parametrization (5.11) and to the γ-dial of Section 5.4? Careful — this is subtler than it looks: in an equilibrium (Bayesian) framework there is no learning rate, so which part of Section 5.2's scaling prescription survives, and in what combination?

(b) What is the order parameter for the modular-addition task? What does the posterior distribution of a single neuron's input weights look like on each side of the transition, and which figure of Section 5.2 does the ordered side resemble?

(c) What are the main computational techniques? List them, and match each to the section of these notes where its ancestor appears.

(d) What parameter is tuned to cross the phase transition in the paper's phase diagrams?

(e) Where did the time go? Grokking is a statement about training time, yet the paper computes a static equilibrium ensemble. How does a first-order transition in an equilibrium free energy produce delayed, abrupt generalization in a training run? Compare, line by line, with the metastability discussion for the Ising perceptron in Section 2.4.1.

Solution

(a) A Bayesian two-layer network f(x)=∑i=1N​ai​ϕ(wi​⋅x) whose readout prior (set by the output-layer weight decay) has variance E[ai2​]=σa2​/N; the limit taken is N→∞ together with σa2​→0 — the paper's "mean-field scaling" — plus the EK (dense-data) approximation. The subtlety: at equilibrium, only the induced prior on functions matters. For the linear readout, a prefactor κ in f=κ∑i​ai​ϕ and a prior variance σ2 for ai​ enter the function-space prior only through the product κ2σ2 (a Gaussian change of variables). So the mean-field parametrization (5.11) — prefactor 1/N, order-one weights — corresponds to bare readout variance ∝1/N2, while variance σa2​/N at fixed σa2​ would be precisely the standard GP scaling of Section 3. The mean-field regime is the additional suppression σa2​→0. Meanwhile the other half of Section 5.2's prescription — the learning-rate rescaling (5.18) — has no equilibrium counterpart at all: the learning rate drops out of the stationary distribution (Section 2.5). In the language of the γ-dial: gradient-flow scalings are classified by (prefactor, initialization, learning rate) jointly, but their Bayesian shadows are classified by the single combination κ2σ2.

(b) The overlap Φ(w) of a hidden neuron's input weights with the teacher-relevant directions — for modular addition, the Fourier coefficients of w on ZP​ (the warm-up (Gromov 2023) says which ones matter). The sharper statement is about the single-neuron posterior P(w): in the GFL phase it is a single Gaussian centered at Φ=0; in the mixed phase it becomes a mixture, with a finite fraction of neurons condensed at Φ=0 and the rest still Gaussian. The order parameter jumps discontinuously: first order. The ordered side is a finite-temperature cousin of Figure 5, where the measure over neurons condenses onto the low-dimensional structures realizing the target.

(c) (i) Noisy training → Gibbs posterior (Section 2.5); (ii) mean-field decoupling of the posterior into readout ⊗ hidden-layer factors, with neurons coupled only through averages (this section); (iii) the self-consistent "adaptive" kernel Qμν​=σa2​⟨ϕ(w⋅xμ)ϕ(w⋅xν)⟩posterior​, whose defining equation has exactly the structure of (5.27) — the kernel depends on a posterior that depends on the kernel; (iv) saddle-point evaluation (Section 2.3); (v) a variational Gaussian-mixture ansatz, needed precisely because a first-order transition means several competing saddles; (vi) the EK approximation for the data average (Section 4.6). Note what is absent: in the main text the data averaging is done by EK smoothing, not by the replica trick of Section 2.3.2.

(d) Primarily the sample size n at fixed temperature: below a critical number of training facts the disordered (memorizing) phase is dominant and the network never generalizes; above it, the mixed phase wins. (The transition line lives in the (n,temperature) plane, so it can equally be crossed by tuning the noise level or weight decay at fixed n — but the grokking narrative crosses it in n.)

(e) In equilibrium there is no time; the free-energy crossing itself is instantaneous. The time-dependence of grokking is the dynamical lag of a first-order transition: Langevin training equilibrates quickly within the metastable disordered basin — which is enough to drive the train loss to zero (memorization is easy there) while test accuracy stays at chance — and only much later escapes to the thermodynamically dominant mixed phase, whereupon test accuracy jumps. This is precisely the Ising-perceptron story of Section 2.4.1: the information needed to generalize is present in the data well before the dynamics finds the ordered state, so capability arrives "abruptly and later than it should."

6. Non-equilibrium physics, MSRJD, and DMFT

So far our statistical-mechanics toolkit has been an equilibrium one: Gibbs measures, partition functions, and free energies (Section 2), together with limits in which training simplifies to kernel regression (Section 4) or to a deterministic flow of measures (Section 5). This section introduces the formalism that confronts the dynamics of learning head-on. The strategy is borrowed from non-equilibrium statistical physics: write the stochastic dynamics itself as a path integral — the Martin–Siggia–Rose–Janssen–De Dominicis (MSRJD) construction — then average over the randomness (noise, initialization, and, crucially, the training data, treated as quenched disorder exactly as in Section 2.2), and finally extract closed, self-consistent equations for a small set of two-time order parameters: correlation functions C(t,t′) and response functions R(t,t′). The result is known as dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), and it is the third and final incarnation of "mean field" in these notes (recall the callout in Section 5.5): the statics of Section 2 determined scalars self-consistently, the McKean–Vlasov limit of Section 5 determined a measure, and DMFT determines whole functions of two times.

The payoffs in this section are a complete worked application — double descent as a dynamical phase transition in linear regression (Section 6.2) — and a guided tour of the modern DMFT program for deep learning (Section 6.3), whose scaling-law application closes the notes in Section 7. Throughout, we follow the spirit of Altland and Simons (Altland & Simons 2010), which motivates the formalism in condensed-matter language with a good balance of detail and intuition, and we borrow freely from two pedagogical tutorials written for neuroscientists, (Chow & Buice 2012) and (Stapmanns et al. 2020).

6.1 From stochastic dynamics to path integrals: the MSRJD formalism

When we model a system with fluctuations — or deliberately add noise to a deterministic model, as in the Langevin dynamics of Section 2.5 — differential equations become stochastic, and the difficulty of solving them jumps. A stochastic differential equation, at first order for example, takes the form

dtdx​=f(x)+ξ,

where ξ(t) is a (Gaussian) white noise process — additive noise, ξ=ξ(t), as opposed to multiplicative noise ξ=ξ(x,t) — and x=x(t) is now a random trajectory. The noise is entirely defined by the first and second moments,

⟨ξ(t)⟩ξ​=0,⟨ξ(t)ξ(t′)⟩ξ​=Dδ(t−t′),

where the expectations are with respect to the noise ensemble4. Obtaining closed-form solutions for the time evolution of the probability distribution for x(t) is usually challenging. These evolutions can be attacked by the traditional routes — the Langevin and Fokker–Planck descriptions — for which the standard references are Risken (Risken 1996), Gardiner (Gardiner 2004), and van Kampen (van Kampen 2007). The objects of interest here are instead the moments of x(t) and the probability density function p(x,t). Methods developed in statistical physics (in particular those used in perturbative quantum field theory and classical non-equilibrium systems) using path integrals provide a way to calculate these statistical objects. The path integral, or functional integral, approach is convenient for perturbative calculations (expanding around an exactly solvable theory with a small parameter), but also permits importing other tools like renormalization group methods or other explicitly non-perturbative approaches when there is no small parameter, or the expansion breaks down (as they often do).

The conceptual recipe of the MSRJD formalism is short, and worth internalizing before the derivation:

  • write down a discrete SDE, fixing a convention (Ito) that enforces causality;
  • express the transition probability between time steps as a delta function imposing the update rule;
  • assemble the product over infinitesimal steps into a path integral;
  • write each delta function in Fourier representation, introducing an auxiliary response field;
  • average over the noise, then add sources and differentiate to extract statistics.

It turns out that the historic approach of Onsager and Machlup (Onsager & Machlup 1953) is the "Lagrangian" version of this "Hamiltonian"-like approach; the two are related by a Legendre transform, or equivalently by integrating out the auxiliary field. That auxiliary field is aptly named the response field: as we will see below, its correlation functions compute how the system responds to external perturbations, and it is the genuinely new ingredient of the non-equilibrium formalism.

We now give the derivation, quickly but completely. The standard first step is to discretize time for a continuous equation, or simply start with a discrete update rule. Under this discretization x(t)→xi​, where i=1,...,N, so that,

xi​=xi−1​+Δt(f(xi−1​)+ξi−1​),

where Δt is the temporal spacing. We can rearrange this so that the RHS is zero and write the transition probability between steps as delta function, and the product of these representing a trajectory solution. Defining a solution of the stochastic differential equation as x[ξ], an expectation value of an observable A[x] is formally,

⟨A[x]⟩ξ​=∫DxA[x]⟨δ(x−x[ξ])⟩ξ​=∫DxA[x]​δxδX​​δ(X).

We used the shorthand Xi​≡xi​−xi−1​−Δt[f(xi−1​)+ξi−1​] for the constraint imposed at each step. The measure here, is a typical functional path integral measure Dx=∏i​dxi​ with δ(x−x[ξ]) similarly factorized across steps. In particular we also picked a first order finite difference and the convention that the noise is evaluated at the previous time-step, which is called Ito discretization or convention. Many common processes are manifestly Ito, like SGD for example, where the noise drawn at a batch doesn't affect the weights at that iteration. There are other conventions, the most common alternative is Stratonovich (which is more like a midpoint rule), however, Ito has a unit (volume-preserving) functional determinant and other schemes require careful treatment to avoid anomalous terms from the determinant. In our case the matrix is triangular with a unit diagonal. Substituting in the definition of X,

⟨A[x]⟩ξ​=∫DxA[x]⟨δ(∂t​x−f(x)−ξ)⟩ξ​.

Finally, we can use the Fourier representation of the delta, introducing an auxiliary variable x~, which in the continuum is

⟨A[x]⟩ξ​=∫DxDx~A[x]ei∫dtx~(∂t​x−f(x)−ξ).

The final step is the payoff: the noise now appears linearly in the exponent, so the Gaussian average over ξ can be done exactly, ⟨e−i∫dtx~ξ⟩ξ​=e−2D​∫dtx~2, leaving the MSRJD functional integral

⟨A[x]⟩=∫DxDx~A[x]e−S[x,x~],S[x,x~]=∫dt[−ix~(∂t​x−f(x))+2D​x~2].

Four structural comments, each of which does real work later:

  • The partition function is one. Setting A=1, the integral is just ∫Dx of a normalized probability: Zdyn​=1, with no sources. Unlike in equilibrium, all the physics lives in correlation functions, obtained by coupling sources to both x and x~ and differentiating — compare the Zdyn​=1 starting point of Section 6.2.
  • The response field earns its name. Perturbing the drift, f→f+h(t), changes the action by i∫x~h, so
R(t,t′):=δh(t′)δ⟨x(t)⟩​​h=0​=⟨x(t)ix~(t′)⟩.

Correlators of x~ compute responses to kicks. Causality is built in: R(t,t′)=0 for t<t′ (the Ito discretization is what guarantees this, along with ⟨x~x~⟩=0).

  • Two-time observables. The natural objects of the formalism are the correlation function C(t,t′)=⟨x(t)x(t′)⟩ and the response R(t,t′). In equilibrium they are not independent: the fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT) locks them together, TR(t,t′)=−∂t′​C(t,t′) for t>t′ (with T=D/2 in our normalization) (Kubo 1957; Kubo 1966). A measured violation of the FDT is therefore the standard diagnostic that a system is genuinely out of equilibrium — the warning light used to great effect in Section 6.2.
  • Onsager–Machlup. The action (6.7) is quadratic in x~, so the response field can be integrated out exactly, giving the probability of a trajectory as P[x]∝e−2D1​∫dt(∂t​x−f(x))2: the Lagrangian form promised above, in which the most probable path extremizes a classical action.

Exercise 6.1 (The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and the FDT). (a) Fill in the noise average leading to (6.7). (b) For the linear drift f(x)=−kx (the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process), compute the stationary correlation and response functions, either by Fourier transforming the quadratic action or by solving the SDE directly: C(τ)=2kD​e−k∣τ∣ and R(τ)=θ(τ)e−kτ. (c) Verify the fluctuation–dissipation theorem TR(τ)=−∂τ​C(τ) for τ>0, with T=D/2. (d) Explain, from the discrete-time construction, why ⟨x~(t)x~(t′)⟩=0 and why R is causal.

Solution

(a) The white-noise measure is Gaussian with ⟨ξ(t)ξ(t′)⟩=Dδ(t−t′), so ⟨e−i∫x~ξ⟩=e−2D​∫x~2, and collecting terms in the exponent gives (6.7). (b) The linear SDE is solved by x(t)=∫−∞t​dse−k(t−s)ξ(s) (stationary state). Then C(τ)=∫−∞t​ds∫−∞t′​ds′e−k(t−s)−k(t′−s′)Dδ(s−s′)=2kD​e−k∣τ∣ with τ=t−t′. Adding a perturbation h to the drift shifts the solution by ∫−∞t​dse−k(t−s)h(s), so R(τ)=θ(τ)e−kτ. (c) For τ>0: −∂τ​C=2D​e−kτ=2D​R(τ), i.e. TR=−∂τ​C with T=D/2. (d) In the discrete construction each delta function propagates information strictly forward in time (Ito: the noise at step i−1 affects xi​, never earlier variables). Diagrammatically, ⟨xx~⟩ is a retarded propagator; ⟨x~x~⟩ would be a closed loop of retarded propagators, which vanishes — equivalently, "a response to no perturbation is not an observable." Causality of R is the same statement.

6.2 Double descent as a dynamical phase transition

As a complete worked application of the formalism, we describe recent work of Li and Goldenfeld (Li & Goldenfeld 2026), which uses dynamical mean-field theory to analyze the double-descent phenomenon and classifies it as a dynamical phase transition, all within the simplest possible setting: a teacher–student model of linear regression. Even this very simple model requires a long calculation, but the paper is quite readable despite the overhead. The headline: in the under-parametrized regime the optimization process is ergodic and relaxes to a finite-error solution, while the over-parametrized regime is a non-ergodic phase with genuinely non-equilibrium dynamics — an initial memorization stage leaves a persistent memory of the initial conditions and confines the dynamics to a subspace around the initialization. The diagnostic is the response function R(t,t′) of Section 6.1 — how a perturbation at time t′ affects the model's state at time t; the same object appears as a Green function in quantum mechanics, signal analysis, and information theory. In the under-parametrized regime the response function decays: no memory. In the over-parametrized regime it saturates at a finite value: persistent memory of initialization. Consistently, the first regime obeys the fluctuation–dissipation theorem (Kubo 1957; Kubo 1966; Goldenfeld 2018), while in the second the FDT breaks — the standard warning light, flagged in Section 6.1, that a system has gone out of equilibrium. The model here is quite simple, and the authors propose that the frameworks here may generalize across architectures, with different universality classes based on the variations of the task, proposing random feature models with multiplicative (state-dependent) noise as an extension, with the hopes of eventually attaining an RG framework for interpreting phase transitions in neural networks.

6.2.1 Model definition and formalism

Notation. We transcribe the paper into the conventions of these notes: P trainable parameters, n training samples, learning rate η, teacher weights w∗, student weights w^ (with response fields w~), and the overparametrization ratio

ν:=P/n

as control parameter — the reciprocal of Section 2's load α=n/N, so that the over-parametrized phase is ν>1. For readers consulting the paper, the dictionary is:

these notesLi–Goldenfeld (Li & Goldenfeld 2026)
P (parameters)d
n (samples)N
ν=P/nα=d/N
w∗, w^, w~β, β^​, β~​
η (learning rate)ζ

The batch-inclusion probability γ, the ridge λ, and the label-noise variance D are as in the paper.

Explicitly, the student and teacher share the same architecture

yμ=P​1​i=1∑P​wi∗​xiμ​+ϵμ

where P is the number of model parameters, μ=1,…,n indexes the dataset with inputs xμ, the wi∗​ are the teacher's weights, and ϵμ is label noise. The thermodynamic limit takes n→∞ and P→∞ with the overparametrization ratio ν=P/n — the paper's complexity parameter — held fixed. The three main regimes are now definable as under-parametrized: ν<1, near-criticality: ν≈1, and over-parametrized: ν>1. We note their optimization procedure, which is SGD with both regularization controlled by λ (set to zero for most of the work) and batching controlled by the binary indicator variable sμ​ which is drawn for each point in the dataset with probability γ,

w^i​(t+1)=w^i​(t)−η∂w^i​(t)∂[21​∑μ=1n​sμ(y^​μ−yμ)2+2λ​∥w^∥22​]​,

From here they construct the MSRJD integral exactly as in Section 6.1; taking functional derivatives and averaging over the disorder (the dataset, the initialization, the batch selection, and the label noise) yields the correlation and response functions that are the main objects of study. We skip most of the details, but it is worth displaying the starting point — the dynamical partition function for gradient flow, equal to one just as promised in Section 6.1:

Zdyn​=∫Dw^(t)i=1∏d​δ[−∂t​w^i​(t)−μ=1∑n​sμ(t)d​xiμ​​(k=1∑P​d​xkμ​​(w^k​(t)−wk∗​)−ϵμ)−λw^i​(t)+ji​(t)]=1.

We want to highlight the general structure of this equation as a path integral over an action with sources coupled to both the "physical" parameter fields and the response fields,

Zdyn​[j,j~​]=⟨∫Dw^(t)Dw~(t)exp(Sdyn​+i=1∑P​∫j~​i​(t)w^i​(t)dt+i=1∑n​∫ji​(t)w~i​(t)dt)⟩,

which is a very common object to see in statistical field theory! In general Sdyn​ will hold all of the microscopic details of the theory, and this is a unique case with a fairly tractable model. In general we are not so lucky. The expectation value denoted by angled brackets is averaging over the input dataset {xμ}μ=1n​, the initial condition w^(0), the stochastic sampling sμ​(t), and the added label noise {ϵμ}μ=1n​. For comedic relief we also write their full dynamical function integrated over quenched disorder:

Zdyn​​∝∫DB(t)∫DQ(t,t′)exp(−iw~∂t​w^−λPQ2​(t,t)−PQ1​⋅Q^​1​−PQ2​⋅Q^​2​−PQ3​⋅Q^​3​−PQ4​⋅Q^​4​−2n​logdet(γQ2⊤​−γQ4​+δQ1​+D​γ2Q3​γQ2​−γQ4⊤​+δ​)+j~​w^+jw~+∫∫dtdt′k∑​(w^k​(t)−wk∗​)Q^​1​(t,t′)(w^k​(t′)−wk∗​)+iw^k​(t)Q^​2​(t,t′)w~k​(t′)+∫∫dtdt′k∑​iw~k​(t)Q^​3​(t,t′)iw~k​(t′)+∫dtk∑​iw~k​(t)Q^​4​(t)wk∗​),​

Where they have split integral measure over the dynamical fields as DB(t)=Dw^(t)Dw~(t), and introduced new notation DQ(t,t′):

DQ(t,t′)=(2πP​)4DQ1​(t,t′)DQ^​1​(t,t′)DQ2​(t,t′)DQ^​2​(t,t′)DQ3​(t,t′)DQ^​3​(t,t′)DQ4​(t)DQ^​4​(t).

Each of the Q variables represents a particular correlation function between two variables.

6.2.2 Overview of results via training and generalization error

They define the generalization error as a mean squared error (MSE)

εg​(t)=⟨(P​1​i=1∑P​xi0​[w^i​(t)−wi∗​]−ϵ0)2⟩

After taking the thermodynamic limit, the generalization error is expressed in terms of the equal time correlator C(t,t) determined from the DMFT equations and D, the noise variance:

εg​(t)=C(t,t)+D

They find two forms of this equation and propose a third, a scaling relation near the critical point. At λ=0 for ν<1, the asymptotic error is:

εg​(t→∞)=D(γχ+1)=1−νD​.

Note the pole as criticality is approached. The quantity χ=∫0∞​R(τ)dτ is the susceptibility; it is well-defined only when the response function decays, i.e. only in equilibrium. Its appearance here signals that in this phase the response to perturbations of the initial conditions really does decay: asymptotically, the system carries no memory of its initialization.

The non-ergodic phase with persistent memory is captured by the asymptotic generalization error depending explicitly on the retention of the initial condition C(0,0) and still showing sensitivity to ν→1 analogous to the ν<1 regime near criticality:

εg​(t→∞)=ν(ν−1)C(0,0)​+ν−1Dν​,

where fully, C(0,0)=⟨w^2(0)⟩+r. The term ⟨w^2(0)⟩ is the variance of the initialization and r is the mean-squared norm of the ground-truth parameters per dimension. Note that here, the response function does not decay, because we carry memory of the initial conditions. It saturates at R(τ→∞)=νν−1​, which they call the ergodicity-breaking degree, quantifying the persistent memory of a perturbation applied to the initialization.

They also show similar trends with the training error, namely for ν<1 the error is asymptotically finite, as the model is still attempting to approximate the solution, while for ν>1 the training error vanishes as initialization-dependent memorization ensures the model always performs accurately on the training data. They write training error as

t→∞lim​εt​(t)=(γχ+1)−2εg​(t→∞).

For ν<1 it simplifies to D(1−ν), while again, for ν>1, the system is no longer at equilibrium and the susceptibility χ=∫0∞​R(τ)dτ diverges, which drives the training error to zero.

To characterize the critical behavior of the model near ν≈1, they calculate the critical exponents (σ,ϕ) and propose a scaling function. The first part is relatively straightforward, where from Eqs. (6.18) and (6.19), one finds εg​(t→∞) diverges from both sides ν→1±. This suggests the scaling εg​(t→∞)∼∣1−ν∣−σ with an exponent σ=1 in DMFT. We remind the reader that these are asymptotic long-time steady-state results and both training and generalization error are time-dependent. Since the saturation time is ν-dependent, a general feature of phase transitions is a dynamic scaling data collapse should be present near the transition (Goldenfeld 2018). They make this argument and propose a scaling ansatz of form:

εg​≈∣1−ν∣σD​F(4∣1−ν∣ϕ(γt)​),

where they introduce a new critical exponent ϕ and write the universal scaling function F(z), and γ is still the probability of samples being included. They make two observations about the form of F near and at the critical point. First, near the point, ν→1± corresponds to z→0, they argue the singularity in front must be absorbed into F and it takes the asymptotic form F(z)∼zσ/ϕ. Second, at ν=1, since the generalization error grows in time instead of saturating, ϵg​(t)∼(γt)σ/ϕ. The exponent ϕ therefore characterizes this growth in training time. Notably, the form of Eq. (6.21) implies a characteristic time scale, which they denote τ(ν)=(γ∣1−ν∣ϕ)−1 to describe convergence in the scaling of the error. Since the error grows, we would expect this to diverge as ν→1, which it does, and is an iconic signature of a phase transition, called critical slowing down. In MC calculations for lattice systems for example, this shows up in the autocorrelation time increasing, and requiring more time to get uncorrelated samples as we approach the critical point. A great deal of energy goes into designing methods to circumvent this slowing down when attempting to measure precise values of critical exponents using MC techniques, and motivates the choice of entirely different paradigms like RG flow or conformal bootstrap where applicable (Goldenfeld 2018).

Exercise 6.2 (Double descent in the lab). Simulate the model of this subsection: teacher w∗∼N(0,rIP​), inputs xμ∼N(0,IP​), labels yμ=w∗⋅xμ/P​+ϵμ with noise variance D; student w^ trained by the update (6.11) with ridge λ=0 and full batches (γ=1), from w^(0)∼N(0,σ02​IP​). Take P=200 and ν=P/n∈{0.5,0.9,1.1,2}. (a) Plot training and generalization error against time, and verify the asymptotics (6.18) and (6.19) — including the divergence of both branches as ν→1: double descent, resolved in time. (b) Probe ergodicity breaking: run two clones from initializations differing by a small random δw^(0), and track the normalized separation ∣Δw^(t)∣2/∣Δw^(0)∣2. Verify that it decays to zero for ν<1 but saturates for ν>1 — at the predicted plateau (ν−1)/ν, the paper's ergodicity-breaking degree, measured in twenty lines of code. (c) Near ν=1, extract the relaxation time of εg​(t) and check for the critical slowing down τ∼∣1−ν∣−ϕ of Eq. (6.21).

Solution

(a) With full batches and λ=0, gradient descent converges for η<2/λmax​(XTX/P); keep η a safe factor below. The late-time errors match (6.18) and (6.19), and plotting εg​(t→∞) against ν traces the double-descent peak at ν=1 from both sides. (b) The clone separation obeys the linear dynamics Δw^(t+1)=(I−ηXTX/P)Δw^(t): it decays iff the sampled covariance XTX has full rank, i.e. iff n≥P (ν≤1). For ν>1 the covariance has a null space of dimension P−n, and the projection of Δw^(0) onto it survives forever; for an isotropic perturbation the expected surviving fraction is (P−n)/P=(ν−1)/ν — precisely the paper's ergodicity-breaking degree R(τ→∞). (c) The relaxation time is set by the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of XTX/P, which by Marchenko–Pastur closes like (1−1/ν​)2∼∣1−ν∣2/4 near threshold, so one expects ϕ≈2; compare with the paper's measured exponent and with the collapse ansatz Eq. (6.21).

6.3 Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT)
